title: Ravens Week 9 Rookie Report: Vega Ioane Returns From Injury, Joe Fagnano Struggles
full_text:
Several members of the Baltimore Ravens' 2026 rookie class saw extended action in last Thursday's 33-10 road loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 9 . They are in an AFC North division in which every other team has a record above .500, and after falling to 4-5, they deservedly sit at the bottom of the standings heading into next week.
Drafted and undrafted first-year players saw extensive playing time in all three phases. The only rookie who was a healthy scratch was fourth-round wide receiver Elijah Sarratt, while fifth-round running back Adam Randall wasn't activated from short-term injured reserve in his fifth week of eligibility. Seventh-round defensive tackle Rayshaun Benny is on the practice squad and has yet to be elevated.
Here’s an overview of how these rookies performed in their late taste of NFL regular-season action.
The first-round interior offensive lineman made his return to the lineup much sooner than expected after only missing one game with an MCL sprain. Ioane played all 56 of the Ravens' snaps on offense and didn't look hobbled when executing his blocking assignments on runs, screens and in pass protection.
Good work on the frontside. Just a tough reach for Vega Ioane to get playside shoulder of the 0T. Not sure who it is, but he tilts his body and gets his playside shoulder into the gap that makes overtaking damn near impossible. Still a solid run pic.twitter.com/5NwMH5rjgt
The second-rounder saw a reduction in his playing time on defense, with his 22 snaps in that phase of the game being the third lowest of the season. While Young didn't fill up or even log a stat in the box score, his underrated grunt work as a stalwart run defender didn't go unnoticed as he played a key role in limiting the Jaguars' rushing attack to a season-low 77 yards.
Despite playing nearly 60% of the Ravens' total offensive snaps with 32, the third-rounder didn't get any chances to make plays in the passing game, as it marked his first game without being targeted. Lane didn't play on special teams at all and was called for a false start once. The scope of the passing game was quite limited, overall.
The fourth-rounder was back to playing near his average number of offensive snaps for the season, with 30, and recorded his first reception since Week 4, before he sustained a hand injury. Hibner reeled in the first of his two targets for a five-yard gain and first down on the Ravens' second drive of the game. His second target came on what would've been the Ravens' biggest play through the air of the game on a trick play, but he wasn't able to corral the pass after it got tipped on its way to him.
With starting outside corner Nate Wiggins inactive with an illness , the fifth-rounder dressed for the game after being a healthy scratch last week, but didn't log any playing time on defense in his third straight appearance. Rivers was only on the field for a single snap on special teams and made it count by recording his second assisted tackle of the season on the last kickoff of the game in the fourth quarter.
The fifth-rounder played his fewest offensive snaps since Week 2 for the third week in a row with just nine, and he had his four-game streak of recording at least one target and one reception snapped. While he didn't log either, Cuevas saw the field for nine snaps on special teams, tied for the second-most of his career.
The sixth-round specialist had another strong outing with five punts for 241 yards, with an average of 48.2 yards per punt and a long of 55. Eckley had one touchback and was able to pin the Jaguars back inside their own 20-yard line three times, with the deepest being at the opposing three-yard line on his very first boot.
The undrafted free agent went from being thrust into his first regular-season action off the bench in Week 8 after both Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley went down with injuries in the first half to making his first career start on a short week. As if the odds weren't already stacked against him, he was dealing with an ankle injury of his own, inclement weather, and the Ravens' offensive line struggled to run the ball or hold up in pass protection long enough for him to regularly get through his progressions in obvious passing situations. Fagnano went 10-of-18 for 60 passing yards, no touchdowns, two interceptions and a passer rating of 22.7. Despite being hobbled, he was able to pick up a pair of first downs with his legs, with one coming on a surprise zone read and the other on a nine-yard scramble where he made a defender miss in space.
Fagnano takes it himself and the family was loving it ❤️ JAXvsBAL on Prime Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/3DX2OXT7JT
The undrafted free agent saw a slight reduction in playing time from last week but still saw the field for the second-most defensive snaps of the season with 25, which accounted for a season-high 44.6% of the team's total. His 23 snaps on special teams ranked first among all rookies and were the third-most on the team. Burke was very impressive as an edge setter against the run, where he consistently stacked and shed blockers on his way to recording three total tackles, including a pair of solos.

title: The Expert Who Helped Lamar Jackson Negotiate His Last Ravens Contract Believes End Could Be Near
full_text:
Almost no one was privy to the inner-workings of the Ravens’ long-and-arduous contract negotiations with Lamar Jackson, dating back to 2020, with an MVP already to his name, once eligible for his first contract extension.
General manager Eric DeCosta, now having quite a miserable time building a sustained winner, led the charge on a process that would take years to complete and was unlike any other first-time QB extension for a superstar in NFL history. It would include a non-exclusive franchise tag and trade demand and collusion case along the way. DeCosta was aided by cap chief Nick Matteo – who has authored some of the ugliest contract structures in the NFL in recent years ( hence the worst cap situation in the NFL ) and team president Sashi Brown, once he took over for legendary steward Dick Cass after he retired.
As for the other side of the table, it was and still is just Lamar Jackson and his mom.
No agent. No marketing guru. No other voice.
And Jackson was seeking counsel from DeMaurice Smith, head of the NFLPA at the time, and Mark Levin, who for roughly 25 years oversaw the Salary Cap and Agent Administration department of the union, in charge of regulating agents and helping them negotiate deals and serving as the PA’s foremost expert on the Collective Bargaining Agreement that governs economic engagement between labor and management.
Levin was Team Jackson’s de-facto agent in the process and a beacon available to them to discuss comparable contracts around the league and structures and guarantees and intricate language. He was available on the other end of the Zoom when they wanted to mull no-trade clauses and no-franchise tag clauses (both of which they successfully obtained) and when they got an $84M poison pill cap charge for 2027 (with a $75M dead cap) that effectively makes Jackson a free-agent after the 2026 season.
Levin was as plugged in on cap and contract matters are anyone on the planet for a generation, and even after retiring from the NFLPA last year, top agents seek his counsel regularly and he assists many more formally as head of Pro Football Consulting. Before taking over the salary cap department at the NFLPA, he oversaw the salary cap and contract negotiations for the Washington Commanders and understands these matters from all perspectives.
He’s continued to follow Jackson’s ongoing saga with the Ravens closely , and their inability to make even a modicum of headway on getting him extended to a new deal back in March of 2025, when it was imperative on the heels of Josh Allen’s extension in Buffalo. Levin predicted basically everything that was to come this summer and fall when he joined me on “The Daily Flock Show” in May to analyze Jackson’s stalemate with the Ravens.
So, with Jackson injured again and the Ravens noncompetitive without him, with a bloated roster that should have been purged before the trade deadline and one of the worst offensive lines and some of the least-proven overall offensive talent in the NFL looking forward, Levin has a strong feeling about what’s next between this two-time MVP, and the Ravens.
Levin knows these individuals quite well and how they operate and was inside these talks and how personal it got at times, unlike almost anyone else on the planet. Like other experts who have discussed this matter with us, it seems obvious to Levin that Jackson will command $70M a season or more, with massive guarantees (even despite his injuries; didn’t impede Dak Prescott, for instance), and Jackson can and will call his own shot in regard to where he plays.
“I would be surprised if he's on the team next year,” Levin told me on “The Daily Flock” this week. “I'd be surprised … Unless the Ravens change their course and agree to make him the highest paid or the second highest paid quarterback on a on a legit structure, legit deal - not with a lot of fluff and window dressing - I just don't see him on the roster next year.
“I think they're just going to have to, you know, for the Ravens’ sake, hopefully trade him and get some good compensation for him, as opposed to just outright cutting him and not getting anything. But I just don't see him on the roster this year. And I think that, based on what's happened this year, you know, it might be time for the Ravens fans to buckle up … and look at a rebuild. They're in a bit of a pickle.”
I’d put Levin’s assessment of the situation up against anyone’s.
Jackson has simply smiled and check-mated the Ravens all along, DeCosta reverted to a trite talking point about being “optimistic” about signing Jackson before the season even as the QB spurned him again, and if the Ravens haven’t paid him what it would take to secure his services by now, it’s beyond fair to suspect they might never again.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Cap Bizarre Deadline By Trading For A Starting Center, For The Second Time In A Month
full_text:
Executives around the NFL strongly suggested the Ravens would not do the obvious and logical thing and start shedding bloated veteran contracts at the trade deadline.
The front office was viewed as too stubborn, full of far too much hubris , to be a seller, and they were correct. But few could have predicted – even as bizarre as things are now in Baltimore – that they would give away their starting kicker to the Falcons, in essence, Tuesday and then trade for a starting center for the second time in a month, this time Atlanta’s Ryan Neuzil. This after trading what could end up being a top 40 pick in 2028 as part of a baffling package for concussed Eagles offensive lineman Cam Jurgens, whose time at center for Baltimore has coincided with an already terrible line hitting new lows with three QBs hurt on about 12 snaps in Week 8.
Yeah, this ain’t the Ozzie Newsome Ravens, not by a long shot.
The Ravens (losers of four straight) have allowed 33 points or more in three straight games for the second time in franchise history (2025) and have failed to score 14 points in four-straight games for the first time ever. And this is what they come up at the deadline.
Numerous NFL executives suggested to us this month that teams had interest in 32-year-old running back Derrick Henry. He's being hung out to dry by the offensive line with no chance to gain yards without Lamar Jackson at QB – and Jackson is most certainly done for the season on IR . Left tackle Ronnie Stanley, receiver Rashod Bateman and defensive lineman Calais Campbell were also identified as prime candidates to be dealt with Baltimore failing to look like a professional operation under overmatched rookie head coach Jesse Minter and facing sweeping roster questions with the worst salary-cap situation in the NFL.
The decision not to have already added kicker Jake Moody to their active roster had no reasonable justification , and after a desperate deal for Jurgens – who is effectively locked in for 2027 at a $17M salary – adding another center, this one a pending free agent, is odd.
Neuzil, 29, is a late bloomer who has strong ties to Ravens offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford and is a former Falcons undrafted free agent who has managed to hang around on futures deals and low-level contracts before getting an extension prior to 2025. The Ravens tried this already with former Falcons fringe lineman Jovaughn Gwyn at center, which struck evaluators around the NFL as a stretch, and he was lost for the season in Week 3.
Center has been a massive issue since the Ravens let stalwart Tyler Linderbaum leave as a free agent. The Ravens have had a new offensive line combo almost every week, the signing of free agent guard John Simpson has been tragic, and they do have first-round pick guard Vega Ioane back from injury (he remains the best center on this roster) and have also looked at youngster Emery Jones at guard.
There is a strong case to be made to bench Simpson (guaranteed at least $5.5M in 2027); but one would think Jones and Ioane would be the starting guards in that scenario. As bad as Jurgens has been adopting to Baltimore’s run fits and with all their communication issues up front, it would still be remarkable, even by this front office’s pathetically-low recent standards, to do that. Of course, with Jurgens’ deep medical history, having cover at center is quite important, too.
Neuzil has started every game at center this season and ddi the same in 2025, making about $4M. (They could have saved a bunch of money and a bunch of draft picks - and maybe had a decent OL - had they executed this trade, oh, I don't know, in May?)
He has 38 career starts. The Ravens shipped out failed offensive lineman Andrew Vorhees and a sixth-round pick in 2028 for him. They think loading up on comp picks is cute and figure someone will sign Neuzil to a decent free-agent deal this winter that will bring back a pick in 2028 that is higher than the sixth they parted with.
The Ravens also released blocking tight end Nick Vannett on Tuesday – the loss of TE Durham Smythe has been significant – and brought back fullback Lucas Scott, with it obvious for weeks more of a true lead blocker was needed for Henry. They let All Pro fullback Pat Ricard, who told me how badly he wanted to stay in Baltimore on "The Daily Flock Show," leave for the Giants in March, where he reunited with former coach John Harbaugh and is in first place in the NFC East.
Meanwhile the Ravens' playoff odds continue to sink and none of Tuesday's transactions are going to help much with that.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Failure To Secure Kicker Jake Moody To Active Roster Baffles NFL Execs
full_text:
The Ravens losing kicker Jake Moody – who they had been grooming as a possible replacement for struggling youngster Tyler Loop - is the latest roster blight and bizarre decision for a front office that is making it their brand lately.
Whether or not Moody solidifies himself in the league remains to be seen, but getting the chance to kick in Atlanta, a dome team, in a division in which weather isn’t nearly as big of a problem this time of year (NFC South) will certainly help his chances. The fact that the Ravens made zero effort to add Moody to their active roster not only at the time they signed him to the practice squad to replace Loop, who was struggling mightily before his groin injury last month, but at any point since, is difficult to fathom.
Moody booted a 50-yard field goal in the rain in Thursday’s latest debacle, a 33-10 loss to the Jags (their fourth straight). He is someone Ravens kicking guru Randy Brown identified back in the summer as a potential replacement for Loop if the youngster could not get more consistent in his second season. Baltimore originally brought in Moody to serve as competition before the season began and then signed him back to the practice squad in-season as Loop began to miss chip-shot field goals and struggled with clutch kicks (though he did hit a game-winner Week 3 in Brazil).
Loop could still return from injury to kick this season, but it was strongly implied that Moody could be preferred to him prior to the groin situation emerging after a loss to Cleveland in Week 6. Loop continued to struggle with kickoffs, too, and rookie head coach Jesse Minter – looking totally overmatched so far – expressed serious frustration with Loop prior to him being placed on Injured Reserve.
“We'll continue to work with him and continue to try to put him in position, but we need to make second-half kicks,” Minter said after his miss at Cleveland. “You could argue that second-half missed field goals are no different than turning the ball over in those situations. So, [that's] definitely something we want to keep striving to be better at."
The move to Moody was about performance more than anything else. And now they have neither kicker, and may have to turn to someone like aging Nick Folk, who the Falcons just cut.
According to multiple personnel executives we’ve chatted with in recent weeks, the state of kicking is bleak and there are few options on the street. Moody looked good in Washington to finish last year, kickers can be late bloomers, he has a pedigree as someone the 49ers invested a Day Two draft pick in, he had a nice preseason, and there are limited options. So the fact that other teams were watching him closely shouldn’t have been lost on the Ravens, but then again they seem to be a fog since last season.
“Atlanta is kind of rebuilding, they want to go with a younger guy with more upside,” one NFL personnel exec said, explaining the dynamic. “And the Ravens have to know there isn’t anything out there. They were just looking at the options before they brought Moody in. There aren’t enough good kickers right now. So if you have one, you need to protect yourself.”
By that he means, keep him signed to the active roster.
The Ravens merely elevated Moody from the practice squad to the active roster for last week’s game, but his roster spot remains on the PS. There was nothing stopping them from just giving him a 53-man roster spot once they knew he was taking over for Loop (most likely for the duration of the season if he was any good). Instead, they abstained and any team could contract Moody at any time with an offer on their active roster, and the Falcons pounced.
“It’s an unforced error,” said another longtime NFL personnel exec who acquired multiple kickers from various means over his career. “No other way you can put it. What the (heck) is going on over there? How does that happen in the NFL? He makes that kick Thursday, just sign him to the active roster …
“If you are this kid (Moody), would you rather be going out there to kick in Baltimore and Pittsburgh and Cincinnati in November and December, out in all of that (weather), or in Atlanta? DeCosta never thought about that? Maybe the other kid comes back (Loop) and he can do the job, but there aren’t enough kickers out there to be giving them away.”
Executives around the NFL have been calling out the Ravens implosions in real-time going back to pulling out of the Maxx Crosby trade in March for alleged health concerns, and with their lack of traction getting MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson signed to contract extensions, putting them in a perilous spot in 2027 . DeCosta has had nothing short of a failure 2025/2026, it seems obvious to other NFL GMs they should have been marketing veterans for sale well ahead of Tuesday’s trade deadline, in a robust way, and serious questions are being asked about the stewardship and direction of the franchise.
They have massive potential roster questions looming at QB (pending where Jackson wants to be next season), as well as left tackle, center, cornerback and safety - for starters - and an untenable salary cap situation to boot. Probably safe to add kicker to that mix, as well.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: The One Contract-Extension Candidate The Ravens Must Approach Now Amid A Lost Season
full_text:
The Ravens have fallen far short of their goals thus far in 2027, hence rookie head coach Jesse Minter, looking largely overmatched thus far, vowing to take corrective measures with his defense ahead of Monday night’s game.
They have not met their overarching goals on offense or defense or special teams. They are the worst second-half team in the NFL, where coaching staffs are measures, resulting in poor results across the board . They prizes generating explosive plays and not surrendering them almost above all else, and rank 25th on passes allowed over 25 yards and have a -3 explosive play differential. They have allowed four more touchdowns than they have scored.
General manager Eric DeCosta built a failure offensive line that played no small role in three quarterbacks getting hurt and Lamar Jackson has suffered two critical injuries already. As we have been pointing out, the player-development fails are pretty sweeping as well (again, the Orioles and Ravens are so stubborn and similar it’s galling), with very few breakout players and the bulk of the team not performing to the level of how they are being paid, and or where they were draft, part of why they should be sellers at Tuesday’s trade deadline .
Minter and his novice staff were supposed to relate better to players and help develop a draft class that all made the team (except for the final pick) plus two undrafted free agent rookies. The inability to not choke away leads – Minter has made it worse – and get more from the roster were the underlying reasons John Harbaugh was cast aside ; he looks like the NFL Coach of the Year with the Giants.
And there is one other way to measure this failed campaign. DeCosta has just three blue-chip players, not on their rookie contracts, signed beyond 2027 – Nnamdi Madubuike, Zay Flowers and Kyle Hamilton. After letting a host of impact youngsters depart as free agents last year, it’s also a terrible sign how few players are making the case for contract extensions this offseason. Yeah, it really is that bleak.
There appear to be only three potential candidates, and there’s only one that I’d be actively trying to approach now, with some of the savings from Madubuike’s contract restructure, to invest in right now:
He is the breakthrough player, and he’s the only breakthrough player.
Especially among those who will have three or more accrued seasons come 2027, making them eligible for a new deal. Mike Green shows some flashes but DeCosta’s horrid record with edge players draws natural skepticism. Devontez Walker has gone backwards and injuries have also hurt others and Nate Wiggins has yet to flash even a modicum of ball-skills at corner and might not fit this scheme ( Marvin Lewis pointed some things out ) and even buying low on him, at that position, ain’t cheap.
Simpson should get a chance to replace Roquan Smith as this becomes more of a lost season and wear the green dot. They need to find out as much about everything he can do. The athleticism has always been there, there’s more pass rush to explore and he brings energy and thump. He should be the priority and seeing how he and Teddye Buchanan fit together the best has to become an overarching goal for Minter.
DeCosta loves to keep throwing money at his first-round picks hoping they eventually make him look good, so beware Wiggins after year three. Might make more sense to finally bench Marlon Humphrey or relegate him to slot-only and see if TJ Tampa can stay healthy and play outside and try to pay him sooner rather than later.
Roger Rosengarten has become more erratic and vulnerable and the overall quality of the offensive line has sunk dramatically since he entered the league. The Ravens have a long history of letting offensive linemen walk in free agency – just happened again with Tyler Linderbaum in March – and if he wants to take a team-friendly, league average deal, great, but starting tackles rarely want to do that because they can get vastly overpaid on the open market.
I would be more inclined to make the rest of this group play it out and prove it. But Simpson would be a priority, now.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: 5 Winners and 6 Losers From Ravens' Primetime Loss To Jaguars
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens dropped their fourth straight game this season in Week 9 on Thursday night because they weren't able to upset the visiting red-hot Jacksonville Jaguars, who pulled away from them late in the first half and never looked back as they handed their host a humbling 33-10 home loss.
They came into this game as heavy underdogs after placing their top two quarterbacks on injured reserve with physical ailments they suffered four days prior. It was going to be an uphill battle anyway; they tried to slice it, and pulling off an upset would've required tremendous discipline and playing complementary football in all three phases, and they did anything but.
With the loss, they fell to 4-5 and remain in last place in the division, where they rightfully belong given how they've played the past month and how banged up they've been on offense.
Here are several Ravens players and coaches who stepped up and showed out, and others who made some costly mistakes from coaching and execution standpoints.
The eighth-year veteran had his most productive game on offense of the season thus far and the second in which he recorded 70-plus rushing yards. He led the Ravens with 85 yards on nine carries, with the bulk of it coming on a 65-yard scoring sprint in the fourth quarter. Hill also caught all three of his targets for seven receiving yards and had some impressive reps in pass protection, picking up blitzers.
65-yard touchdown for Justice Hill! Tune in on Prime. pic.twitter.com/kvYH0fyt7X
In his first appearance as a Raven in place of injured second-year pro Tyler Loop, the more experienced fourth-year pro had a confidence-inspiring performance. He drilled his lone field goal attempt from 53 yards with room to spare and, right down the middle, did the same on his extra point attempt and didn't have any kickoff infractions.
Jake Moody from 53 yards in his first game as a Raven... JAXvsBAL on Prime Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/TRegHRPfdk
For the fourth week in a row, the Ravens held the opposing team's rushing attack in check to under four yards per carry and didn't give up 100 yards on the ground collectively for the fifth time this season. They had three different players record a tackle for loss and did a great job of setting the edges and flying to the ball.
KYLE HAMILTON IN THE BACKFIELD. 😤 Tune in on Prime. pic.twitter.com/zVAwmOhArG
The rookie specialist was a reliable weapon for the Ravens in the battle for field position, pinning the Jaguars' offense inside their own 20-yard line on three of his five punts, with a long of 55 and an average of 48.2 yards per punt.
The second-year pro gave up a big play in the first half of this game and made one in the second half that gave the team life. On the one he allowed, he got beat inside for a 53-yard touchdown by Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington, who was playing in the slot when the Ravens dialed up a blitz. With the Ravens trailing by 17 points late in the third quarter, he not only made a tackle for loss by blowing up a wide receiver screen, but he also forced a fumble that gave the offense the ball back at midfield.
FORCED FUMBLE!!! RAVENS RECOVER!! Tune in on Prime. pic.twitter.com/Wmg8gj76dO
In more ways than one, it felt like the undrafted rookie never really had a chance to succeed in his first career start for a myriad of reasons, including his ankle injury, weather conditions, poor pass protection, pre-snap penalties that put him behind the sticks, and the players around him not making plays. Nonetheless, he didn't play well in his own right, by his admission, going 10-of-18 for 60 passing yards and two interceptions.
Although the four-time Pro Bowler finished the game stronger than he started it, by blowing a coverage on the Jaguars' opening offensive drive of the game, that sprung a blocking tight end for a 52-yard gain, set the wrong kind of tone for the type of game it'd wind up being. Humphrey earned Pro Football Focus' highest coverage grade on the Ravens' defense with a 68.9, had the fourth-highest overall grade with a 70.1 and had two pass breakups.
The three-time Pro Bowler led the team with 19 receiving yards on a pair of catches, but it was what he did before the snap and when lined up under center that landed him on this list. He was one of two veteran leaders on offense who committed one of two back-to-back false starts that derailed the Ravens' second possession of the game. Andrews also fumbled a fourth-and-1 snap on a failed quarterback sneak late in the third that resulted in a turnover on downs.
The Ravens got virtually little to no pressure on the Jaguars' quarterback, Trevor Lawrence, who wasn't sacked at all and was hit just once. Far too often, he was allowed to survey the field and launch bombs over their heads for chunk gains, completing 8 of 10 passes of 10-plus yards for 193 yards and a touchdown. The one good thing they were able to do up front to disrupt Jacksonville's passing attack was bat down three passes at the line of scrimmage, with two coming from two-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike and the other from fellow seventh-year veteran Broderick Washington.
While no quarterbacks were hurt during this game, compared to all three getting banged up the week prior, this blocking unit struggled to consistently execute once again. Even though the Ravens recorded their fourth-highest rushing yardage total of the season (172), the bulk of that production came late in garbage time, with the Jaguars up by 30 points and conceding anything that let them bleed the clock.
Pass protection continues to be a struggle for this unit, as they allowed an already physically compromised quarterback to get sacked three times and hit four times. The viral crash-out from offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford on the sideline that was caught on camera was completely warranted given how poorly his unit performed at home in primetime.
Ravens offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford is not happy 😳 (📺 PRIME) pic.twitter.com/KwgRWOSgDM
The second-year specialist continues to not provide much juice as a returner, and he fumbled the ball deep in Baltimore territory on a kickoff that set up the Jaguars' third touchdown drive of the game in the fourth quarter.

His coverage on the Ravens and other NFL teams has been featured on Heavy.com/sports, Maryland Sports Blog and most recently Baltimore Beatdown from 2021 until 2025.

title: Final Ravens NFL Trade Deadline Big Board
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens have every reason to be as motivated to sell at the NFL trade deadline as any team in the league.
Okay, not as much as the Chargers or Colts or the Titans … but certainly as much as the Eagles as a team with Super Bowl aspirations that has never looked the part this year. The Ravens are the dregs whether they want to admit it or not – they have lost four in row being outscored by 70 points, they have allowed 33 points or more in three straight games and failed to score 14 in four straight and it’s far more likely than not that Lamar Jackson doesn’t see the field again this season no matter what the scoop jockeys peddle.
They are the worst second-half team in the NFL, the coaching staff has been totally overwhelmed thus far, and if you are looking for individual success stories from a player-development standpoint, well, there is first-round pick Vega Ioane and, pending unrestricted free agent linebacker Trenton Simpson, and Zay Flowers has had halves of football with Jackson that have been otherworldly and been largely invisible otherwise.
If you are looking at critical tiebreakers – the isn’t going to be an AFC North title, sorry – well a .286 strength of victory is third-worst on the AFC and Baltimore has just two AFC wins (lowly Colts and Titans) and their -47 scoring differential is better than only the Colts, Titans, Dolphins and Chargers. And they are 7-15 playing games that Jackson doesn’t start since he became their starter. They get whipped in the trenches with regularity and this offensive line – the “construction“ of which is a fire-able offense in and of itself – is probably not done getting QBs hurt.
But none of that matters in Owings Mills (that’s what the access merchants are saying ), where they talk a big game and hype-up an alleged winning culture that died years ago. So what does that mean as the trade deadline looms Tuesday afternoon? Here’s where things stand:
Cam Jurgens – Not nearly as good at center as Ioane, and will command $17M next season anyway. Dealing a potential top 40 pick for him in 2028 – while he was concussed, by the way – would get you fired soon enough in an organization that was serious about winning.
Jacoby Brissett – Giving up essentially fourth-round value for him may also blow up in their face. His ability to stay upright behind this offensive line could be a real issue and lacks the legs to help unlock Derrick Henry in a broken run game.
None - Yeah, this is over. The payroll is bloated beyond belief already, this was supposedly an elite roster all along and, while desperately needing all the picks they can muster to try to get out of an ugly salary-cap crunch (explained in detail in “The Daily Flock” below), they have already mortgaged future drafts. Even trying to make the case for a cheap veteran kicker like Joey Slye doesn’t make sense anymore and Jake Moody did boom one from 50-plus Thursday.
None – To this point, hubris and stubborn remain the rule for a front office that has been unable to steward this sinking ship anywhere but down – consistently – since the 2023 AFC Championship Game.
Henry – Longtime NFL general manager Marty Hurney explained on “The Daily Flock” how open he would be to moving the future Hall of Famer (“I’m not calling but I sure am listening,” is how he framed it). We have talked to execs around the NFL who believe Henry is cooked in Baltimore behind this line (3.4 yards/carry the last four weeks) and needs to go. Mark Levin, former Commanders salary cap guru who oversaw salary cap and agent administration for the NFLPA for roughly 25 years, also believes the team should try to get a fourth-round pick for him. He's 32, where RB careers expire, and being run into the ground.
Ronnie Stanley – His cap situation is ugly no matter what with $28M in dead cap hoveering in 2027. Now would be the perfect time to see what Carson Vinson could do and as a former Pro Bowl left tackle, in a shallow OL market, execs tell me he could fetch a decent return.
Rashod Bateman – Hasn’t cracked 300 receiving yards this season is still good for catching less than two of every three balls he sees and has never living up to his draft billing outside of what was really one 10-game stretch in 2024. With a $13M salary next year, he’s gone one way or the other in the spring.
Calais Campbell – At age 40, this is his last hurrah. Being a part of a rotation with the Lions or Chiefs would seem to make a lot of sense, for starters, or even a return to Jacksonville where he spent his best seasons after they just lost a dominant defensive tackle for the season.
Others – No one I talk to thinks any winning team would want anything to do with the contracts Roquan Smith or Mark Andrews, though the Ravens should be highly motivated to jettison both by any means possible.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: How Team-First Dion Dawkins Made Bills' Trade for Amani Hooker Possible
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills were seeking help on the defensive side of the ball, and they needed an offensive tackle to help make it happen.
The Bills traded for Tennessee Titans' safety Amani Hooker prior to Tuesday's NFL deadline, but there was one minor issue that needed resolution before the deal became official. Buffalo needed $4.4 million in available salary cap space to accommodate the addition.
Per Spotrac, the Bills opened the day with only $3.8 million in room against the spending limit. That's where starting left tackle Dion Dawkins entered the equation.
Buffalo requested a salary conversion for Dawkins as a means of creating cap space. Per Spotrac, the Bills converted $7 million of his 2026 salary into a signing bonus. That transaction frees $5.3 million in room in addition to the $3.8 million in space that already existed.
With Hooker essentially being a replacement for Chauncey Gardner-Johnson, who quickly wore out his welcome, it's worth noting that Buffalo is absorbing a $2.3 million of dead money on this year's cap due to the failed free agent signing.
After playing a road game on Monday night, and not arriving home until the wee hours of Tuesday morning, the players had the day off while Bills' general manager Brandon Beane was busy working the phones.
"We had to restructure Dion today to make that happen. And so, appreciate Dion," said Beane. "He was out at a community event. My man [Manager of Football Admin and Ops] Ryan Moore tracked him down and we got it, we got it done. As soon as we knew that this was getting close to the finish line, we sent Ryan to where Dion was."
There was some confusion in public circles about the salary conversion deadline. The Bills processed the conversion for Dawkins on Tuesday as Monday's deadline was only for players who were changing teams in a trade.
Dawkins is currently in the second season of a three-year contract extension worth $60.06 million. The 32-year-old Dawkins was selected in Round 2 by the Bills at the 2017 NFL Draft.
"Appreciate Dion and his reps helping us out and getting this to the finish line," said Beane.
In a rare occurrence , Dawkins was inactive on Monday night against the Minnesota Vikings. He did not practice last week and was scratched due to a ribs injury .

title: Dalton Kincaid, Spencer Brown Fighting New Injuries After Bills' Primetime Week 9 Win
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills posted a 23-6 road win on Monday Night Football in Week 9, but it didn't come without a few bumps and bruises along the way .
Starting right tackle Spencer Brown and tight end Dalton Kincaid were already battling injuries that popped up during the Bills' two-week swing through Los Angeles and Las Vegas.
Despite nearing full strength heading into the November 9 road game against the Minnesota Vikings, Brown and Kincaid remain on the injury report in Week 10 thanks to new problems.
Both players apparently sprained an ankle going up against the Vikings' vaunted defense.
"That was a physical game on Monday night and we kinda knew that [would be the case]," said Bills' head coach Joe Brady prior to Wednesday's walkthrough practice in Orchard Park. "Right now it's really like, we're two days out of the game so we're walking today at practice. We're gonna have to kinda get a feel of where everybody is, and I'll have a better answer for you guys come Friday."
Kincaid and Brown were listed as limited participants on the week's first official injury report with the ankle issues. The Bills are technically on a short week with a road game against the New York Jets set for Sunday, November 15 at 1 p.m. ET.
The Bills' primary pass-catching tight end went down early in the fourth quarter while blocking for wide receiver DJ Moore along the sideline.
Kincaid left the game for a quick evaluation, and he returned with his ankle taped later on the same possession. With 8:12 remaining in the game, Kincaid snagged a short pass to convert a 3rd-and-3 in Vikings' territory.
The good news is Kincaid appears to be completely in the clear concerning the ribs/chest injury that popped up during the third quarter on October 18. He was a full participant for Buffalo's last two Week 9 practices, and he also ditched the red non-contact jersey.
After missing the November 1 game due to back issues, the fear was that Brown reaggravated the problem on Monday night against the Vikings.
Although he appeared wincing in pain following a couple different plays throughout the night, his ankle, and not his back, was the culprit. Brown apparently suffered the sprain during the Bills' second possession blocking for a James Cook carry.
"I'm just playing football right now. It's a tough sport. That's why I play it. That's why I love to play it. I look forward to next week and getting back out there again," said Brown after the win .
Brown played 77 snaps in the victory, sitting it only the final three kneel-downs by backup quarterback Kyle Allen.

title: Will Amani Hooker Play in Week 10? What New Bills Safety Said About Potential Debut
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills made a huge addition to their defense right before the trade deadline with the trade for Amani Hooker.
With a little over an hour to go before the deadline stuck, general manager Brandon Beane completed a trade with the Tennessee Titans for Hooker, giving up a second-round pick while also receiving a fifth-rounder in return.
The trade was mostly well-received by experts , and it was almost universally well-received from a Bills fan base that has been yearning for that kind of move for years now.
With Hooker now in the fold, the next question is: will he make his Bills debut in Week 10 against the New York Jets?
Hooker spoke to the media on Wednesday for the first time since the trade and he made a definitive statement about his status against the Jets.
“Oh I’m gonna play on Sunday. Yeah. I’ll be ready to go," Hooker said .
It'll be a quick turnaround for Hooker, who will have just five days to prepare to take the field. But he's a smart player, so he should have a fairly good grasp of the playbook by Sunday.
While we know he's going to suit up, what we don't know is if Hooker will play a full complement of snaps. That will likely be determined as the game wears on.
Hooker has been a mainstay on the field during his career.
Over seven games with the Titans this season, the veteran safety has played on a whopping 99% of snaps, and the last time Hooker played fewer than 90% of snaps in a season was his sophomore campaign in 2020.
It didn't take long for Hooker to see just how much Bills fans love their team. In fact, he said he felt it as soon as he stepped off the plane and saw all of the people wearing Bills gear.
“I can just really feel the love here for this team," Hooker said.
Hooker is going from a Titans fan base that has been criticized for not having enough passion for its team, to a Bills fan base that is one of the most dedicated in the NFL.
Hooker is a versatile safety, but he does his best work on the back end as a free safety, where he's solid in coverage and has a nose for the football, as evidenced by his five picks this season and 17 interceptions over his career.
That's a perfect fit for the Bills , who haven't gotten much turnover production from their safeties. In fact, C.J. Gardner-Johnson is the only Bills safety to record a pick this season and he's no longer on the team.
Buffalo also sports the fourth-worst pass defense in the NFL and has given up 28 completions of 20-plus yards this season. Hooker should help the Bills there, also.

title: Bills' Amani Hooker Trade Grades: Not Everyone Loved Buffalo's Deadline Day Deal
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills made one of the biggest trades on deadline day when they swung a deal with the Tennessee Titans for safety Amani Hooker.
The trade saw general manager Brandon Beane give up a second-round pick in exchange for Hooker and a fifth-round pick.
Buffalo had a clear need at safety and needed a big move. Hooker is not a superstar player, but he is on that next tier and should prove to be a very nice upgrade for the Bills' defense that desperately needed a boost.
Now, let's see how experts from different media outlets graded the move. We've also provided our grade beneath those.
Walder comes in with the lowest grade in our round-up. His biggest issue with the Bills' trade is the price.
"So Hooker is an upgrade at a position of need for a Super Bowl-contending team and will save them a few million per year relative to the market. But is that worth a second-round pick? It strikes me as rich. Hooker is a good player but not a star -- he has never been a Pro Bowl selection or All-Pro and only snuck into Jeremy Fowler's NFL evaluator survey of top safeties in the 'also receiving votes' category. As a result, the compensation here is a bit steep," Walder said.
A second-round pick is expensive, especially for a safety who is very good but not elite. However, we also have to remind ourselves that the pick is going to be late in the second round, which basically makes it a third-round pick, so there's that.
Adding to that, the Bills received a fifth-round pick back, and we also know that Hooker is under contract for two more years following this one, so that also softens the blow.
Patra was a fan of the deal because of the fit with Hooker. He didn't think the price was too much.
"I love the fit. Buffalo can now become much more multi-faceted on the back end with Hooker’s arrival," Patra explained. "The price wasn’t exorbitant for a player still under contract for two additional years with no guaranteed money. Yes, giving up a Day 2 pick is tough, but assuming it’s at the back of Round 2 while the Titans pick is at the front of Round 5, it’s not that far of a fall to get a potential difference-maker come January."
The Bills had one of the worst pass defenses in the NFL and that's something Hooker will help with given his strength is playing on the back end.
Hooker's ball-hawking ability is huge, also, as the Bills had just one pick from their safeties combined this season and C.J. Gardner-Johnson, who is no longer with the team , had the pick.
Pereles thinks the trade for the Bills was "expensive," but all of the positives Hooker brings to the table is enough to justify the price, as is the Bills keeping up with other Super Bowl contenders who made big trades.
"The Bills saw several other Super Bowl contenders making significant win-now moves and decided to make their own on deadline day, acquiring safety Amani Hooker and a 2027 fifth-round pick from the Titans for a 2027 second-round pick," he explained.
"It's a big move for a player in the middle of his best year: Hooker has five interceptions this year, including three off Joe Burrow in one game. Other Bills safeties have one pick combined. He is a versatile defender who's willing to tackle -- a strong addition to a Bills secondary that needed help. It was expensive, but worth doing. Buffalo got significantly better Tuesday," Pereles added.
Reports suggested the Titans weren't interested in trading Hooker ahead of the deadline, so Beane was going to have to overpay a bit to pry him away from Nashville.
I'm pretty sure that if Bills fans had to choose between the trade that went down and nothing at all, they would choose the former. Fans have been wanting Beane to do something significant for years now and he finally did it.
I love this trade for the Bills.
Yes, a second-round pick is a lot, but it's basically a third-round pick because the Bills' selections are going to be at the end of rounds. Buffalo also got a fifth-round pick back, and they are getting a player who is under contract for two more years .
Hooker is also a well-rounded player with his ability to play strong or free safety, and even in the slot. He is also good in coverage and against the run, as evidenced by his Pro Football Focus grades of 75.2 in coverage and 83.9 in run defense, ranking 10th and 13th among safeties, respectively.
Hooker thrives most at free safety and has a nose for the football. As we previously noted, the Bills had just one pick from safeties in 2026, and we know also sports one of the worst pass defenses in the NFL and the defense has given up 28 plays of 20-plus yards, an issue Hooker can definitely help fix.
The Bills needed a big trade to help their defense and this was as close to one as Buffalo could get. Hats off to Beane for getting it done.
Daniel Popper, The Athletic: A-
Walter Cherepinsky, Walter Football: A
Eric Edholm & Frank Schwab, Yahoo Sports: B+

title: NFL Trade Breakdown: Why Bills’ Move for Amani Hooker Makes Perfect Sense
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills finally got the safety help fans have been clamoring for. So, how should we grade the deal?
The Bills did not rest on their 7-1 mark and win on Monday Night Football , as they traded for Tennessee Titans safety Amani Hooker on Tuesday. Buffalo gave up a second-round pick and also received a fifth-rounder.
But just how impactful can he be? If recent years show, he can make a major difference in the Bills' secondary.
Since 2024, Hooker has 10 total interceptions, including a league-best five in 2026. Three of them came against Joe Burrow and the Bengals in Week 8.
Buffalo, as a defensive unit, has six, which is tied for the 13th-best in the NFL.
His 81.0 PFF grade is sixth-best in the league thus far this season. That is boosted by a coverage grade of 75.2. But he also has an outstanding 83.9 run defense grade, the highest of his career.
Other advance metrics also show how valuable he is roaming the secondary. He's allowing a career-low passer rating of 60.2 and given up just one touchdown on the year.
A veteran with true centerfield skills can be helpful in Buffalo's defensive backfield. Especially being paired up with a young safety.
In the midst of his third season, Bishop has shown flashes of being a viable starting safety. But ever since the Bills let C.J. Gardner-Johnson go following his suspension, Buffalo has needed to fill a hole at secondary.
Hooker does that. And the contract that he's on allows him to be paired with Bishop in the future. At only 28 years old, Hooker is now under contract with the Bills through the 2028 season.
According to Spotrac , his deal brings a cap hit of $4.47 million for the remainder of 2026, before jumping to $10.28 million and $13.5 million over the next two seasons.
The Iowa product also provides a great hybrid tandem with Bishop. Coming out of Utah, many believed Bishop would be best suited at strong safety. But early in his career, he has looked better in coverage as a free safety.
And although Hooker's ball-hawking skills are stated, the 2026 season has shown he can be a successful player in the box as a strong safety.
With Leonhard in his first season as defensive coordinator, the unit has had its ups and downs . Now, he's got a dynamic playmaker playing the position he once did in the NFL.
Leonhard may have played 10 years in the league, but his career pales in comparison to Hooker's. Because of his NFL experience, though, that could help him guide Hooker in picking up the defense in short order.
Hooker may not be known to most people nationally. But make no mistake: Buffalo acquired a player who may be ready to break out onto the scene with his new team.
Leonhard was named one of our three clear winners from the Hooker trade.
Tennessee, thank you. 💙 Eight years ago, my dream came true & Nashville became home. I grew up here as a player and as a man. Ms. Amy Adams Strunk and Mike Borgonzi, thank you for believing in me and giving an opportunity to play the game i love. I am truly blessed to have had…

title: Confirming 'Aggressive' Bills Pursued DT, Another Big-Name Safety Before Amani Hooker Trade
full_text:
If Buffalo Bills general manager Brandon Beane hadn't come away with a big addition at safety at the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday, it wouldn't have been for a lack of trying.
Of course, Beane did get his man when he pulled off a trade with the Tennessee Titans for safety Amani Hooker — and he did so right before the deadline passed.
But safety wasn't the only position the Bills were targeting.
According to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler , the Bills "were clearly the most aggressive team" on deadline day, and they were even looking at adding a defensive tackle along with a safety.
"The Bills were clearly the most aggressive team on a somewhat slow deadline day. Word surfaced early Tuesday that Buffalo was clearing cap space via contract restructuring," Fowler explained. "Teams believed Buffalo was seeking impactful safeties and/or defensive tackles."
Before landing Hooker in the trade with the Titans, Fowler says the Bills were also after another big-name safety, and more specifically, Arizona Cardinals safety Budda Baker.
Fowler says the Bills offered a "compelling package" but ultimately the Cardinals just didn't want to trade Baker.
"The Bills made a play for Baker with what one source considered a compelling package. Arizona did not want to trade him because he's viewed as the heart and soul of the team," Fowler said.
Literally minutes before the Hooker trade was reported, there was another report that the Bills had "checked in" on Baker, so there is more than one piece of evidence for Buffalo's interest in him.
There were rumblings in the lead up to the deadline that Baker was open to being moved to a contender , but it was consistently said that the Cardinals didn't want to trade him. That turned out to be true.
Fowler provided some more details on Beane's pursuit of Hooker.
While trying to land Baker, the Bills were also hard at work on a deal for Hooker, who the Titans initially planned to keep. But, after a little back and forth, Beane got the deal done.
"But the Bills were also working on Hooker, and it took a counteroffer of sorts to make that deal happen," he said. "The Titans originally resisted an offer for Hooker, whom they planned to keep; coach Robert Saleh loves him on the roster. But Buffalo tried again, pushing it to the finish line."
If you're wondering why the Bills gave up a little more than you'd expect for a safety, there's your answer. Beane had to overpay to convince the Titans to let Hooker go, and he was able to get the job done.
Right before the deadline, Beane told the Associated Press' John Wawrow that "I'd like to think I always try to be aggressive," which drew an eye roll from Bills fans.
We can't say we blame them for reacting that way given the lack of success Beane has had near the deadline during his tenure. It sure hasn't seemed like he has been all that aggressive in the past.
But the Bills general manager was clearly very aggressive this time around, and while the Hooker trade doesn't erase all of the issues fans have had with Beane over the years, it certainly buys him some grace, especially if the trade pans out.

title: Bills' Week 9 Snap Count Analysis: Keon Coleman, Davison Igbinosun Winning Big
full_text:
It took players from all corners of the roster for the Buffalo Bills to post a 23-6 road victory over the Minnesota Vikings on Monday Night Football in Week 9.
Seventeen different players saw at least 10 snaps on offense for Buffalo. On defense, 18 players logged 13 snaps apiece or more.
In all, the Bills' offense was on field for 80 snaps in the November 9 win . The defense was needed for only 48 reps as Buffalo dominated the time of possession by a 42:32-to-17:28 margin.
Here are the major Week 9 snap count observations highlighted by wide receiver Keon Coleman and cornerback Davison Igbinosun.
Bills' official Week 9 snap count vs. Vikings 📋 ( @NFL345 ) pic.twitter.com/hCkH168nQI
The Bills were without the starting left side of their offensive line as left tackle Dion Dawkins and left guard Alec Anderson were scratched due to injuries. Replacements Tylan Grable and Austin Corbett proceeded to play every single snap during the primetime win.
Totaling 80 reps apiece, Grable and Corbett were even on the field for the Kyle Allen kneel-downs as the Bills ran out the clock with starters Connor McGovern, O'Cyrus Torrence and Spencer Brown looking on from the sideline.
Bills' safety Cole Bishop was the lone defensive player to log all 48 snaps. Safety Damar Hamlin, who left briefly due to cramping , was second with 44 reps.
He's gone from the doghouse to the penthouse in a matter of 12 months. Benched last November for lateness and lack of professionalism, Coleman has revived his career under head coach Joe Brady .
Coleman, a 2024 second-round draft pick, again led all Bills' wide receivers in snaps on Monday night. In Week 8 against the Ravens, he led all skill position players in offensive reps. Against the Vikings, running back James Cook (51) and tight end Dawson Knox (58) were the only skill players to out-snap Coleman (49). Wide receiver DJ Moore logged 47 reps.
Willingness as a run blocker has earned Coleman a 68 percent snap share thus far this season on offense.
Another encourgaing takeaway from Coleman's high Week 9 snap count is that the wide receiver appears to be nearing full health. He was on the injury report last week due to a shoulder issue.
With two starting linemen unavailable against the NFL's top-ranked pass rush, the Bills, taking a run-heavy approach, frequently deployed multiple tight ends.
Buffalo used its patented 13 personnel lining three tight ends up in the formation on multiple occasions. The Bills leaned so heavily on their tight ends that fourth-stringer Keleki Latu, who made his first career touchdown catch, saw a season-high 21 offensive snaps.
Outside of quarterback Josh Allen and the starting linemen, tight end Dawson Knox earned the most offensive reps (58). On field for 72 percent of the action, Knox out-snapped players like Cook and Moore.
The Bills started the game with Knox and Jackson Hawes with wide receivers Moore and Coleman split out. Hawes proceeded to total 46 offensive reps. Dalton Kincaid was on field for 40 snaps.
It seems like eons ago since second-round rookie cornerback Davison Igbinosun was the backup to Maxwell Hairston.
One month into the season, Igbinosun overtook Hairston as the starter opposite Christian Benford, and the high-energy defensive back doesn't appear headed back to the bench anytime soon.
Igbinosun, who has made five consecutive starts, led all Bills' cornerbacks by playing 81 percent of snaps against the Vikings. He also played 80 percent of possible reps in Week 8 against the Ravens.
Over eight games, Igbinosun has registered 29 tackles, eight pass breakups and one interception.

title: Amani Hooker Trade Comes Despite Bills' Back-to-Back Historic Performances on Defense
full_text:
With their victory over the Minnesota Vikings on Monday Night Football , the Buffalo Bills accomplished a feat last achieved during the Super Bowl years.
The Bills now sit atop the AFC at 7-1 overall,  marking the first time the team has won seven of its first eight games since 1993.
And, what’s so special about that?
Well, as mentioned above, it just so happens to be the last time Buffalo reached the National Football League’s pinnacle game: the Super Bowl .
Whether or not that same fate is in the cards for first-year head coach Joe Brady’s squad later on this winter remains to be seen, but there are also a few other special accomplishments that the team achieved on Monday that might bode well for its chances of doing so in a few short months.
In addition to obtaining their fourth win in a row, the defense—yes, the defense—managed to do something that has only been seen in the league a mere 12 times over the last 40 years as the unit surrendered less than 200 yards and 10 points for a second straight game after previously holding the Baltimore Ravens to just 10 points and only 144 total yards of offense the week prior to their most recent 23-6 primetime thrashing of Minnesota on the road.
It was a repeat performance for the ages that was certainly a sight for sore eyes for a team that had previously allowed 28.5 points per game and 386.8 total yards per game through the first six outings of the season this fall.
So, with that said, not only was it an encouraging sign for the Bills’ fanbase to see from Leonhard’s previously struggling group, but the dazzling display put on in Minneapolis on Monday also placed the Bills’ defense in some incredibly good company.
According to Niagara Gazette reporter Nick Sabato, of the other 11 franchises to hold opponents to 10 points or less and under 200 total yards for at least two straight games, two of the teams won Super Bowls: the previously mentioned Ravens in 2000, as well as the Seattle Seahawks just one season ago.
Undoubtedly, those two teams are great to be mentioned amongst. However, furthermore, if Bills Mafia wants to flip the calendar back another year further, then the defense is also on par with the renowned 1985 Chicago Bears’ defensive unit.
According to the Bills’ public relations’ account on X , no team other than the 2026 Bills and 1985 Bears have had a two-game stretch in a season where the defense had multiple sacks and at least three takeaways in each game while also holding the opposing offenses under 200 total yards with no passing touchdowns and a completion percentage under 50% in each contest, as well.
So, with that in mind, the question begs to be asked . . . is Buffalo going to make an appearance in Super Bowl LXI on Valentine’s Day 2027 in February?
Well, given that Bills’ general manager Brandon Beane just sent this April’s second-round pick to the Tennessee Titans in exchange for starting safety Amani Hooker , who currently leads the NFL in interceptions with five entering Week 10, it certainly appears like Brady, Beane, and Leonhard are going all in on winning a “world” championship this season.
It won’t be easy, though, especially considering that Buffalo’s opponents over the final nine games of the regular season are collectively averaging 21.5 points per game, which is much more than the Ravens ( 11.0 PPG ) and Vikings ( 12.3 PPG ) have averaged over their last three matchups.
Needless to say, it’ll be interesting to see how much of an impact the addition of Hooker has on the Bills’ defense moving forward once he gets up to speed with Leonhard’s scheme . . . as well as if the last two weeks were more of a mirage opposite of quarterback Josh Allen’s humming offense or if it’s really the start of a miraculous turnaround moving forward this year.
One way or another, fans are about to find out soon enough .

title: Three Clear Winners, One Loser from Bills' Deadline Trade for Titans' Amani Hooker
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills answered the bell, completing a notable trade prior to Tuesday's NFL deadline.
Addressing the need to upgrade their defensive secondary, the Bills struck a deal with the Tennessee Titans for veteran safety Amani Hooker. It's worth noting, that we listed Hooker as one of the three safeties Buffalo could realistically trade for and remain salary cap compliant.
Buffalo opened a spot in its safeties room by releasing loudmouth Chauncey Gardner-Johnson, who overstayed his welcome by performing poorly and creating multiple extracurricular distractions.
Veteran Damar Hamlin has started the two games since Gardner-Johnson's departure. While Hamlin has performed adequately, and will likely remain in the rotation at some level moving forward, the Bills seemingly desired to add a known difference-maker to the defensive backfield.
Whether or not Hooker can be that addition, time will tell. As for right now, here are three clear winners and one loser from the trade at this point in time.
Hooker goes from a rebuilding team with a 1-7 overall record to a Super Bowl contender that sits atop the AFC through nine weeks. For a competitor, it's like unexpectedly waking up in paradise.
Having spent all seven-plus NFL seasons with the Titans, Hooker will likely feel strange leaving, but he'll certainly be welcomed with open arms in Orchard Park.
Showing gratitude for his time in Tennessee, Hooker issued a X post that ended with "Bittersweet, but excited for what's next." What's next is a starting spot on the Bills' defense for the NFL current interceptions (5) leader.
After playing the position for 10 seasons at the NFL level, Bills' defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard knows what to look for in a safety. By trading for Hooker, Bills' brass has given Leonhard a proven piece to immediately plug into his work-in-progress defense .
"He's a player [with] instincts, ball skills. You're going to think I'm describing Micah Hyde, which there are so many similarities of Iowa, taking the ball away. He's just been a very steady player," said Bills' general manager Brandon Beane.
Hooker has 103 career appearances, including 74 starts, since being drafted in 2019. He's not only a free safety. In addition to playing centerfield, he can move up into the box if needed. The versatility, at the least, has to excite Leonhard.
With the pressure high to improve the team for its postseason chase, Beane was able to make fans forget about the failed Gardner-Johnson experiment by adding a safety for a reasonable price. The Bills had to part with a second-round draft pick, but also receiving a fifth-rounder in return softens the blow.
“You gotta find the right partner, which is they have a player that you value, that you feel upgrades your team in some position, and that you can fit in the salary, that you can handle the draft compensation, whatever it is, or player for player, however you do the deal," said Beane.
Making the deal better for Beane and the Bills, Hooker is much more than a half-season rental. The Bills will have the safety under contractual control through 2028.
It's likely the ultimate Catch-22 for Stone, who is reunited with his college teammate.
When the news broke, the Bills' backup safety, who is still on the practice squad , published a X post with two emojis and photo of himself standing alongside Hooker on the field during an Iowa game.
Although his friend will now be in the building, Hooker's arrival eliminates the need for Buffalo to sign Stone to their active roster at this point.
Stone appeared in the last two games as a practice squad elevation, and he made his presence felt. The veteran made six tackles and one pass deflection in Week 8. He played 25 more defensive snaps in Week 9.

title: Bills' Week 10 Injury Outlook for Dalton Kincaid, Spencer Brown, Christian Benford
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills took care of business on Monday Night Football in Week 9, and they appear to have avoided any new serious injuries in the process.
In all, four Bills' players visibly received medical attention at some point during the November 9 victory over the Minnesota Vikings . All four eventually returned to action, but they'll warrant monitoring in Week 10 as Buffalo prepares to visit the New York Jets.
The Bills, who placed wide receiver Josh Palmer on Injured Reserve prior to the primetime kickoff, were without the starting left side of their offensive line in the 23-6 primetime road win.
With left tackle Dion Dawkins and left guard Alec Anderson scratched due to injuries that emerged in Week 8 against the Baltimore Ravens, and seemingly week to week, starting right tackle Spencer Brown was dinged up again on Monday night.
Additionally, tight end Dalton Kincaid apparently rolled his ankle early during the fourth quarter. He was slow to get up, but missed minimal time.
Both Brown and Kincaid were already on the injury report due to other issues.
In the defensive backfield, lead cornerback Christian Benford and safety Damar Hamlin both needed trips to the locker room late in the first half.
Here's what we know about each player with a November 15 divisional road game looming.
After recovering from a back flare-up that kept him out against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 8, Brown picked up a lower body injury against the Vikings.
Brown, who was visibly experiencing discomfort at different points on the field, reportedly rolled his ankle during the first half, and proceeded to grind through the rest of the way. He played every snap until the final three kneel downs.
"I'm just playing football right now. It's a tough sport. That's why I play it. That's why I love to play it. I look forward to next week and getting back out there again," said Brown after the win .
It's important to see how the ankle reacts when the Bills begin prep for the New York Jets on Wednesday in Orchard Park.
Kincaid's ankle was twisted up as he went to the ground blocking for wide receiver DJ Moore along the sideline on a 2nd-and-8 play with 14:12 remaining in the fourth quarter.
Briefly leaving to have his ankle examined and subsequently taped, Kincaid quickly returned later during the same possession. With 8:12 left, the tight end made a nice snag for a five-yard gain to convert a 3rd-and-3.
Kincaid had been on the Bills' official injury report due to a ribs/chest issue that dates back to October 18 against the Las Vegas Raiders. He was upgraded to a full participant in practice leading up to Monday Night Football.
Benford's injury seemingly warrants the most cause for concern out of the four players. He apparently jammed his wrist while taking Vikings' wide receiver Justin Jefferson to the ground following a catch with less than 1:00 remaining in the first half.
The Bills' cornerback got a head start to the locker room while being ruled questionable to return. After apparently checking out satisfactorily , Benford was back on the field for the first snap of the third quarter.
Buffalo pulled Benford for the remainder of the night later in the quarter, but he remained on the sideline in full uniform. Officially logging 28 of a possible 48 defensive reps, he reportedly told Buffalo News' writer Jay Skurski that X-rays on his hand/wrist were negative.
Back in a starting role since Chauncey Gardner-Johnson's dismissal, Hamlin reportedly cramped up right around halftime . As a result, Geno Stone started the third quarter in his place.
Reportedly receiving IV in the locker room, Hamlin was unavailable for the first defensive possession after halftime. Missing only four total snaps, he returned to action with 5:59 left in the third quarter.

title: NFL Week 10 Expert Picks: Will Panthers Hold Off Saints for First Place?
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers still hold the lead in the NFC South race despite losing three games in a row . They are 3-5, which is the same record as the New Orleans Saints.
Those two teams will not have the same record this week, barring a tie. They'll face off in New Orleans for the first time this season. You'll recall that the Saints' peskiness made the division title a lot harder to come by for Carolina last season.
A win keeps the Panthers in first. A loss drops them out for the first time in a long time and it would bring up even more questions.
CBS Sports analyst John Breech predicts a narrow Panthers victory, 23-20. These two teams played two relatively tight games last year, and with how evenly matched they seem right now, this is unsurprising.
His CBS colleague, Pete Prisco , has picked the Panthers in one game all year, and it was the ugly loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Big shocker: Prisco is going with the Saints in this one, 24-21.
"This is an enormous game in the division, even though both teams have just three victories. The winner will be in first place. The Saints beat the Browns last week, while the Panthers have lost three straight. The Saints make it four in a row as Tyler Shough has a big day," he wrote.
Sporting News' Vinnie Iyer is keeping the field-goal difference here, predicting the Saints to emerge victorious, 27-24. "New Orleans dug deep to outlast Cleveland last week and found some needed rushing juice with Audric Estime. They also have the receivers around Tyler Shough to duel Bryce Young and his weapons well. Both defenses have been maligned, but toss a coin toward Brandon Staley," he wrote.
Sports Illustrated's Iain MacMillan isn't willing to make a prediction on the tight matchup, instead saying the best pick is to take the over, thanks to two horrible defenses.
Jeremy Cluff of Arizona Republic thinks the Panthers win a little more handily than others, 28-20. "Bryce Young and the Panthers have lost three straight games, but are still right in the thick of the NFC South race. New Orleans is 1-4 at home. Carolina ends its skid with a big win on the road," he said.
Sports Betting Dime's model predicts a 30-26 win for the Panthers. Dimers' model predicts a 25-24 victory for the Panthers.
What does this tell us? That the margins in this game are unbelievably thin. It's going to be an extremely close contest, with some experts leaning one way and others leaning the other.
The Panthers need to turn the tides, but they have their work cut out for them.

title: Dan Morgan's Seat Should Be Getting Hotter After Panthers' Quiet Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers did nothing at the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday. For a team battling injuries and poor depth in the secondary, that was not the move that most fans were hoping for from the Panthers.
But that is not the only issue. The Panthers' secondary has been a problem for several seasons, and general manager Dan Morgan has not done enough to address it.
The problem with the Panthers' roster extends beyond what Morgan did not do on trade deadline day. It extends to what he has not done to fix the team's secondary in the past.
At some point, the GM needs to be held accountable for the roster he has put together.
Horn and Jackson can play when healthy, but that isn't the issue. The problem with the Panthers' secondary is that there isn't enough depth at cornerback for when those two players are injured.
The Panthers have had some good performances from Horn when he is healthy. Jackson is also a good player for the Panthers. However, as is the case in the NFL, injuries happen and the Panthers should have been better prepared for Horn or Jackson to miss time.
The Panthers have a secondary that is too thin, and Carolina cannot rely on that secondary to get them through any tough spots.
As previously discussed in Panthers on SI's report on Carolina's cornerback injuries, the injuries have exposed how little depth the Panthers have behind their starters.
Morgan had numerous chances to add to the Panthers' secondary in free agency, the draft and now at the trade deadline. Instead, the problems that the team is experiencing in the secondary are the same problems that have existed for several seasons.
That's difficult to overlook.
Morgan can be forgiven for not giving up a lot of assets for a short-term fix to the secondary problems, but it does not mean there are no other holes on the Panthers' roster to fill in order to become a Super Bowl contender.
The Carolina Panthers entered the trade deadline with a 3-5 record but were still leading the NFC South. Carolina still had a chance to win the division, but the team needed to start winning games.
While Carolina did not need to make a blockbuster trade, Morgan could have looked to bring in a solid veteran cornerback to provide some depth at the position.
The Panthers did sign veteran cornerback Jakorian Bennett to their practice squad on November 6, but that doesn't mean the team's depth problems have been solved.
The asking prices on some of those players might have been too high for Morgan's taste, but the Panthers' secondary has been a problem for a while now, and that needed to be addressed long before the trade deadline on Tuesday.
In addition to not making a trade, Morgan's offseason decisions will also be put under a microscope.
The Panthers can't keep blaming injuries for certain positions on the field.
As discussed in Panthers on SI's earlier trade deadline analysis, Carolina couldn't afford to sacrifice valuable draft picks just to make a short-term move. But that doesn't excuse the front office for not having enough dependable options at cornerback.
And if Carolina's secondary is still in trouble and the Panthers can't capitalize on their opportunity to win the NFC South, Morgan will have to answer more than just why he didn't make a trade at the deadline.
Why weren't the Panthers better prepared at certain positions on the field?
