title: Which Texans Players Could Get Dealt on Trade Deadline Day
full_text:
The Houston Texans have just a couple of hours to go until they're on the other side of the NFL trade deadline.
﻿ To this point, things have been pretty quiet in H-Town . And that's led to the belief that the Texans could simply let this deadline come and go without making a move to their roster— which is a very real possibility.
But when taking a step back to look at the Texans' roster ahead of the trade deadline, a select few players around the building might make sense as a potential name to ship out for one reason or another.
Whether it be because that player might have value on the trade market if they were shopped, or if they might simply be a better fit in another situation, four players onboard the Texans feel as if they're the most likely names to be on the move, if a trade really is in play before 3 PM CT.
With that in mind, let's take a look at four Texans players that have the most realistic shot of being traded on deadline day:
The Texans' offensive line has taken a bit of a different shape from the state it was expected to be coming out of the offseason.
Back in the summer, the Texans were expected to start free agent signing Wyatt Teller at left guard in hopes that he would be an upgrade for a struggling unit upfront.
But he's only started in two games this season because of an injury to Ed Ingram, and has instead found his role as a bench contributor that might be better suited for a change of scenery at the deadline.
The Texans could find a suitor that has a starting spot in mind for Teller, get minimal draft capital in return for him, but also salvage a bit of their offseason investment that hasn't panned out quite as well as the front office would've hoped.
It's a win-win for the Texans and Teller, if he's looking for a bigger opportunity heading into the second half of the season. And in reality, this feels like it could be the most likely move of all that we see Houston end up making.
A very similar case here for Braden Smith: someone who the Texans signed to a two-year deal earlier in free agency expected him to start on their new-and-improved offensive line, yet hasn't found a consistent role as a starter since beginning the first four weeks of the season on injured reserve.
At most, Smith has filled in as a contributor in the Texans' jumbo looks on offense. But on a line that also has a solid backup swing tackle in Blake Fisher behind their starting duo of Aireontae Ersery and Trent Brown, Smith's presence in this offensive line room becomes a bit redundant without a clearly determined role.
So rather than let Smith sit in the Texans' offensive line room as a backup for the rest of the season, the Texans could strike on a deal for more value than someone like Teller could be worth, reshuffle their tackle room without Smith, and have a better set of draft assets to build with for this offseason.
Could the Texans value Smith more as a depth piece on their offensive line? Might teams be wary about trading significant assets to an injury-prone veteran tackle? Yes and yes. And those two factors might be what hold up a move getting done here. But it's an idea that's worth considering from Houston's lead decision-makers.
It's always fair to question whether or not a quarterback-needy team could be in the market to add Davis Mills; someone who many consider to be one of the more reliable backups in the NFL. And the idea isn't too outlandish to consider here for the Texans .
C.J. Stroud is playing lights-out through eight games of the season. He's going to get a new contract this offseason, and so is Mills, who's currently in the last year under contract and is due to be an unrestricted free agent in 2027.
If the Texans didn't intend on paying Mills another contract, a deadline move would make sense. Houston can cash in on an expiring contract in the form of a draft pick, and send out a backup who's gotten barely any playing time this year anyways.
However, the Texans could still go out and re-sign Mills this summer. And even if they aren't, the front office may simply see more value in Mills as a backup on their roster compared to whatever they could get back in return via trade. And if that's the case, then they might not deal Mills out at all.
This is simply a case of the Texans suffering from an overabundance at a certain position. And in this case, Houston might have one too many tight ends currently on their roster.
And the one name within that group of tight ends that makes sense to ship out would be Cade Stover.
He was just deemed a healthy scratch just last weekend against the LA Chargers, and with the increased involvement of Marlin Klein in the game plan moving forward, it'll be even harder for Stover to make an impact moving forward.
The solution? The Texans could trade away Stover now, get a minimal return for him, and move forward with a slimmer tight end room that opens up more involvement for Klein, as well as Brevin Jordan and Foster Moreau.

title: Every RB Texans Can Potentially Land at NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Houston Texans are just hours out from the NFL trade deadline–– and nobody knows which direction this team is going to go .
One area on the roster that has been circled as a potential position of interest for the Texans has been running back.
According to Sports Illustrated 's Albert Breer, Houston has been among the teams checking in on "available" running backs around the league before the deadline, along with safeties.
As to who the Texans might have their eyes on is a bit of an unknown. However, when surveying around the league, there are several running backs that could stick out as guys that are potentially available, fill a need on the roster, and within reason for Houston to go out and add for the right price.
So let's do some digging. Which running backs around the league could the Texans truly go out and make a move for?
Let's look at 10 different names at the position around the league to keep an eye on––tiering them as either veteran depth pieces, high-value starters, and longshots that probably aren't on their way to Houston anytime soon:
This would be the range of outcomes to expect for the Texans: not an upgrade that really shakes up the top of the depth chart, but one that could provide some much-needed depth behind the current running back room that's been both shallow and dealing with injuries over the past few weeks.
Each of these guys feels unlikely to claim more than a day three pick in exchange for their services on the trade market. And for the Texans, that's a price tag they could be willing to pay in order to add some much-needed security at running back for a run game that's been stuck in the bottom half of the NFL all season.
The one name I'd keep the closest watch on here is Devin Singletary of the Giants; a veteran runner who would cost minimal assets to acquire, has been in Houston before, and could be the right caliber of back to slot behind Woody Marks and David Montgomery as a reliable RB3 who can produce on the ground and through the air in a pinch.
These two feel like they could be grouped within the next category: they haven't been included in many trade rumors leading up to the deadline, and in all likelihood, probably won't be on the move to the Texans anytime soon.
However, the idea of the Texans pursuing either is at least fun to consider.
Breece Hall was briefly rumored as a Houston target this past offseason as a potential addition to an expansive roster of Iowa State alums, while Ashton Jeanty presents a similar situation to Marvin Harrison Jr., where the front office takes a chance on a young talent who hasn't performed up to expectations in the spot he was drafted.
When stacking up the price tag of each (likely to cost at least a day or two to pick), along with the lack of clear desire or aggressiveness from either team to make a move on these backs, don't hold your breath on the Texans striking on a trade here.
But maybe once the offseason arrives, and the situation continues to look as it does for both running backs, then perhaps the Texans' interest could shift in a different direction––if their backfield dilemma is still in a similar spot.
Here are the big names at running back that everyone's talking about at the deadline: Jonathan Taylor, Saquon Barkley, and Derrick Henry.
Each would be due to command some serious interest in the market if their respective teams decided to aggressively shop them. And for a running-back-needy team like the Texans, they make sense as a suitor that should keep all three at least on the radar leading up to the deadline.
But the realism behind a move for any of these three–– at least from Houston's perspective–– feels pretty out there with just a few hours to go until the buzzer sounds.
For one, there's the cost that each would be due to land from any team interested in acquiring them: a first-round pick appears to be the going rate.
Maybe the Texans would be interested in paying that given their Super Bowl aspirations, but that's still a pretty steep price for an older running back with many miles on the odometer.
But Barkley and Henry have also both been informed by their teams that they won't be traded ahead of the deadline. That creates an even stronger hurdle for Houston to overcome. Taylor might be a different story, but it'd be really hard to expect the Colts to ship out their franchise running back to a division rival like the Texans, even if the package in return was an ideal one.
So if the Texans were to make an addition at running back at the deadline, expect the scale to be a bit smaller than these guys. These top-tier stars might just be out of reach, and if they weren't, their price tag might be a little too steep for Houston's desires.

title: Texans Must Consider a Last-Minute Splash for This Trade Candidate
full_text:
The Houston Texans are right around the corner from the NFL trade deadline–– and there hasn't been a whole lot of chatter surrounding how this team could approach the coming hours .
Some argue the Texans should stand pat with their current group. They're coming off a win building momentum for the second half of the season with an already-talented roster, and investing in another addition to the roster might not be exactly necessary.
Or, there's the argument that the Texans could hit the market as buyers.
After all, this roster isn't perfect, and following their AFC South rival, the Jacksonville Jaguars, peppering the market with multiple moves on Monday , that might add even more incentive for Houston to get aggressive and make a push to make a tweak before the next nine games on the schedule.
But what might the Texans' most splashy move on the trade market be, within reason?
It's hard to really expect the Texans to go out and trade away multiple first-round picks for a superstar talent at this point. And especially for a big move surrounding someone like Jonathan Taylor, who sits right across from them in the AFC South, Houston making a move for his services might be a bit wishful thinking .
But there is one starting-level, acquireable trade candidate that the Texans should have their eyes on leading up to the deadline: someone that could provide an immediate impact for the offense, fills a position of need, and has Super Bowl pedigree that Houston would be sure to love adding as well.
That's none other than Philadelphia Eagles offensive lineman Landon Dickerson, who makes too much sense as a Texans trade target to at least consider in the time before the deadline buzzer sounds.
Now, when looking at the Eagles' perspective of why a Dickerson deal makes sense, it's not too tough to sort through.
Philadelphia is taking a step back by making multiple selling moves by already sending away guys like Jordan Davis and Cam Jurgens. Dickerson fits the mold as a valuable, starting offensive guard who can also net future value for their upcoming retool. That part adds up.
And when surveying around the market, the Texans might just be an ideal trade partner for the Eagles to look towards.
Their offensive line has been steadily improving throughout the season, but could still use further stability with a talented guard like Dickerson; someone who's strong and physically gifted at the position with experience and versatility to play multiple positions.
This season, Dickerson hasn't performed quite as well as he has in years past. PFF places him with the 55th-best overall grade among 77 eligible guards (55.5), along with ranking bottom 10 in pass-blocking grade.
However, perhaps in a new situation out of the Eagles, like in Houston–– a team that seems to be trending up rather than down for the next several weeks–– maybe that could rejuvenate Dickerson to be the high-end guard that he had been during Philadelphia's Super Bowl runs.
The Texans, or any other team that were interested in acquiring him, would be due to only pay him $607,500 in the remaining 2026 salary, but would then be forced to pay upwards of $20 million in each of 2027 and 2028.
Short-term, the costs wouldn't be hard to stomach whatsoever, but could become a bit more challenging after the season. And if anything, that could be what holds the Texans back from pulling the trigger on such a move.
In terms of draft compensation, it's hard to imagine the Eagles being able to net more than a day-two pick in exchange for Dickerson when combining his recent play, injury concerns, and contract implications. And for a Texans team that just gave up a second-round pick for Marvin Harrison Jr. , any more than a third to give up for Dickerson might feel too rich.
But that type of investment might need to be one that the Texans consider in an effort to take their roster another step forward for the second half of the season.
The Jaguars just went out to add a stout defensive tackle from the Eagles that could be due to give the Texans trouble down the line, and maybe adding Dickerson on the line upfront is the best way to counter that.
He can fill in at left guard, allows rookie Keylan Rutledge to shift to the center spot, and gives the Texans a really respectable three-man interior to move forward with for the rest of the season.
The ball is in the Texans' court. Time will tell if they wind up pulling the trigger on a big move like this or similar, or if they instead decide to play it safe without a move at the buzzer.

title: How Jalen Pitre Helped Texans Defense Find Its Identity vs. Chargers
full_text:
After an up-and-down first seven games on the season, the Houston Texans' defense finally looked closer to their elite form in Week 9 against the LA Chargers en route to their dominating 44-22 victory in SoFi Stadium .
Everything was clicking for the Texans' defense compared to some of their recent performances. They got to Justin Herbert for a season-high eight sacks , which led to him completing just 50% of his passes, forced two turnovers, and held the Chargers' offense to less than 325 total yards on the day.
So what changed for the Texans this week? Why was their defense finally able to turn a corner for a solid day of production when stacked up against some of their latest disappointments?
In DeMeco Ryans' mind, a lot of the credit falls on the shoulders of Jalen Pitre.
Pitre, who had been out of the Texans' lineup since suffering an AC joint sprain in Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans, had finally made a return to the defensive side of the ball as Houston's versatile nickelback against the Chargers.
And Pitre really wasted no time making his regular impact. He ranked second on the team for combined tackles on the day with six, with two of those coming as tackles for loss.
DeMeco Ryans spoke the day after the win over the Chargers about the defense's overall performance from the weekend, and unpromptedly spoke about why Pitre's return to the Texans' defense was so valuable on Sunday.
"The defense definitely executed much better when it came down to, specifically, the tackling piece of it," Ryans said. "I thought our guys really tackled well. I thought having Pitre back was really the highlight for me."
"The plays that he's able to make; it really energizes our entire team. Like, the physicality he plays with. Him blitzing off of the edge, making plays in the backfield, really making it hard on opponents, because of his playstyle and where he's aligning all over the field."
It's hard to argue with Ryans. A lot of what the Texans had been missing on their defense over the past several weeks are traits that Pitre himself brings to the table: tackling, consistency, and versatility in the secondary, and hard-hitting bravado.
And that's exactly what he was able to chip in for on Sunday, turning out to be one of the bigger stars on the Texans' defense entirely, and helping Houston's stock on that side of the ball take a much-needed turn in the right direction.
When Pitre is on the field with this Texans' secondary, while the likes of Derek Stingley and Kamari Lassiter are also playing up to their All-Pro and Pro Bowl standards, paired with a commanding pass rush, it quickly becomes tough to attack this defense altogether.
That was exactly the case for the Texans this Sunday, and helped them get back on track with their third victory on the season. And if Pitre is able to lead the way for similar success from this talented Houston defense moving forward, there are due to be a few more wins to follow.

title: Where the Texans Stand 24 Hours Before the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Houston Texans are now less than 24 hours away from reaching the NFL trade deadline.
And to this point, how the Texans might approach their plans in the coming hours is still largely undetermined.
Coming off a Week 9 win at 3-5 and looking to continue building momentum for the second half of their season, there's a chance that Houston goes searching around the trade market in hopes that they can improve this roster from its current state.
There's also a world that the Texans decide to stand pat and play things conservatively at the deadline if there isn't a deal on the table that the front office truly covets. Houston has already made a couple of trades over the past few months as is, so maybe this time of year winds up being a bit quieter than expected for the front office.
The ball is in the Texans' court right now. They've got until 3 p.m. CT on Tuesday afternoon to make any and all trades they may be interested in, and potentially put a finishing touch on this roster moving into the next portion of the regular season.
Let's sort through everything that matters surrounding the Texans' trade deadline situation, and what to look out for in the coming hours as teams begin to scramble looking for any final moves.
While the Texans have been watching from the sidelines on the trade market since their move to acquire Marvin Harrison Jr. , the surrounding AFC South has made no shortage of moves to either double down on their hopes of making a deep postseason run, or in the case of a couple of teams, take a step back and look towards the future.
The Jacksonville Jaguars just added a couple of defensive pieces as of Monday in Jessie Bates III and Davon Godchaux. The Tennessee Titans just shipped out All-Pro Jeffery Simmons as of last week. And the Indianapolis Colts could still be on track for a bit of a fire sale, having already sent out Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, and maybe Jonathan Taylor in due time.
So will that extra activity around the division influence the Texans to go out and make a move of their own? It's certainly possible knowing how much general manager Nick Caserio likes to make a trade every now and then. And it might not be the worst idea to hit the market for a deal either.
If they were persuaded to pull the trigger on something, it feels far more likely that Houston would hit the market as buyers rather than sellers, having just come off a Week 9 win to sit just two games back from .500.
The last we heard on the Texans' interests at the deadline, SI insider Albert Breer linked Houston to potentially target two positions : running back and safety.
Now, as to how significant in terms of scale the Texans are willing to upgrade each position remains to be seen. Maybe Houston goes out to add a star safety like their division rival Jaguars just did less than 48 hours out from the deadline, but having both positions on the radar does make sense.
The Texans' run game has started to look better over the past few weeks since David Montgomery has been out with a groin injury , but could still use another layer of depth and playmaking for the second half of the season.
Houston's safety unit has also dealt with underperformance and injury issues, with their latest concern centering around Reed Blankenship and his concussion/hand injury. So if the Texans felt they needed to find an upgrade at either spot on their roster, now might be the perfect time to address it.
The one name on the Texans' roster who had probably seen themselves in the most trade rumors over the past week was veteran edge rusher Jadeveon Clowney, who ESPN's Adam Schefter reported had been generating interest from teams leading up to the deadline during Houston's bye week.
But while the interest in Clowney might be there, it doesn't make much sense internally for the Texans to consider moving him.
Clowney fits a need on the Texans' defense, is on a flexible and affordable one-year contract, and comes fresh off potentially his best game of the season against the LA Chargers, where he was one of three players to end the day with two sacks. Simply put, Clowney is here to stay .

title: What Stood Out From Texans' Week 9 Snap Counts vs. Chargers
full_text:
The Houston Texans claimed a much-needed win over the LA Chargers in Week 9, commanding their way to a 44-22 blowout, that now puts this team back on track for a potential run in the second half of their schedule with the same record they had at this time last season.
And in the fallout from the Texans' Week 9 victory , we now have a glimpse of how the snap counts panned out for Houston within all three phases, giving us a picture of who played a bunch, and who didn't over the course of their West Coast road trip.
Let's take a look at how things shook out for the Texans and Chargers' snap counts for Week 9, and point out a few aspects that might be a bit notable from Houston's perspective:
For yet another week, the Texans showed that they weren't shy when it came to getting wide receiver Xavier Hutchinson on the field, as he saw a resounding 81% of Houston's total offensive snaps, which was even higher than Nico Collins’s snap share of 73%.
Hutchinson isn't the most dangerous downfield weapon for the Texans to keep on the field, but he is a positive blocker who contributes in the run game, while also providing a reliable set of hands who chipped in for three receptions, 29 yards, and a touchdown as of this weekend.
Another development that sticks out in the Texans' wide receiver room: both Tank Dell and Marvin Harrison Jr. were able to see the field noticeably more than before the bye. Neither eclipsed a 25% snap share in their latest showing against the New York Giants, to now seeing those opportunities doubled in Week 9.
Dell definitely turned in those added snaps for the better day, as he was one of two Texans pass-catchers to reach above 100 receiving yards. But to see both Dell and Harrison Jr. on the field and more involved in Houston's offensive game plan is a positive sign for what's ahead.
It only took four weeks of being a healthy scratch on the Texans' gameday roster, but second-round rookie tight end Marlin Klein finally got back on the field for Houston in Week 9 , where he got a chance to get some reps in a first-year campaign he's been largely limited in.
And it was in this game where Klein saw a season-high 19 offensive snaps with nine on special teams–– which is a significant step forward from how the Texans' usage panned out for him through the first seven weeks.
The only problem arises when factoring in Klein's zero recorded stats in those opportunities. Maybe he can show more in Week 10 against the Cleveland Browns.
The Texans made an underrated addition to their defensive line at the bye when they added recently-cut San Francisco 49ers defensive tackle Naquan Jones; a previous member of Houston's 90-man roster before the season started, and would be one of their toughest cuts heading into Week 1.
But the Texans got their hands back on Jones for the second half of the season. And against the Chargers, they wasted no time getting Jones involved as a rotational piece of their defensive line.
Jones landed just under 40% of Houston's defensive snaps, and was one of five defensive tackles to get at least 33% of the snap share. It was a heavy rotation for DeMeco Ryans' interior this weekend, but a strategy that proved to be effective.

title: Colts Trades Present Massive Opportunities at 3 Vital Positions
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is officially in the rearview mirror, and the Indianapolis Colts were very busy, given that the franchise is at the beginning of a full rebuild.
The Colts traded off defensive tackle DeForest Buckner (San Francisco 49ers), guard Quenton Nelson (Seattle Seahawks), and wide receivers Josh Downs (Kansas City Chiefs) and Keenan Allen (49ers).
With four key players traded away, it drastically shakes up the defensive tackle, guard, and wide receiver rooms for the Colts for the rest of the 2026 season.
With that in mind, let's look at the pecking order for those three positions for Indianapolis and which players will need to step into the fray as the Colts try to make something out of their 2026 season.
The Colts traded Buckner to the 49ers for a 2027 fourth-round pick. Immediately, this took away one of the best defensive players Indianapolis has had over the last seven years.
However, the Colts felt better about this decision after Adetomiwa Adebawore emerged as a candidate to keep for their rebuild.
This led the Colts to extend Adebawore on a two-year, $35 million deal.
The Colts and DT Adetomiwa Adebawore agreed to terms on a two-year, $35 million extension that includes a $13M signing bonus and $22.5M in new money through 2027. Still only 25, Adebawore has a chance to get back to the market again as he enters his prime. The deal was… pic.twitter.com/D4TVQLVbvO
Through nine games, Adebawore leads the Colts with 4.0 sacks and is second in QB pressures (20) to defensive end Laiatu Latu (23). Adebawore will get eight more games in 2026 as Indy's top man in the defensive trenches.
As for Grover Stewart, he'll resume his position as the Colts' premier run-stuffer. Stewart wasn't traded at the deadline, but there was an offer in place that the Colts didn't execute.
Stewart's contract expires after this year, and it's hard to imagine Indianapolis will re-sign him in 2027, especially after trading Buckner.
Jerry Tillery, Tim Smith, and Kevin Givens will round out the room behind Adebawore and Stewart.
In a lost season where the Colts are gearing up for a refresh next year, it's mostly about Adebawore getting more experience as the undisputed top defensive tackle in the Circle City.
After playing eight illustrious seasons for the Colts, Nelson was traded to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.
Trade! The Colts are sending eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . pic.twitter.com/O1EN6vHWSF
Buckner was a big loss for the defense, but Nelson is a future Hall of Famer who was still playing at an elite level upon being traded. However, this gave Indy's 2026 fourth-rounder, Jalen Farmer, the green light to take over.
Offensive line coach Tony Sparano Jr. was one of Farmer's biggest fans during the draft process, and felt that the former Kentucky Wildcat enforcer was a special talent, and made that excitement well-known after he was selected.
It’s officially the Jalen Farmer era in Indianapolis. The #Colts have a new starting left guard for the first time in almost a decade. Lord knows OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr. is excited to get to work. https://t.co/3UctqjGZxD
Farmer hasn't played much this year as the starter, but as expected, he's struggled to fill Nelson's shoes.
Per Pro Football Focus, Farmer has grades of 39.4 overall, 45.7 run-blocking, and 26.8 pass-blocking. He's also allowed seven pressures and three quarterback hits through two games played.
Matt Goncalves remains the undisputed starter at right guard, while Dalton Tucker serves as the swing piece in the room.
The rest of the season is all about Farmer gaining valuable experience to become the left guard of Indy's future.
However, expect him to have big-time growing pains, as he's only 22 and is getting a crash course in what it's like to start in the NFL.
Indianapolis dealt away Downs and Allen, who were both the best wide receivers for the Colts after Alec Pierce was placed on Injured Reserve early in the year with a heel injury.
With Downs and Allen no longer on the roster, Indy's wide receiver corps is incredibly underwhelming, and just might be the worst in the NFL.
This isn't to pile on talents like Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, and Deion Burks, but when we consider Treadwell, Dulin, Burks, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, and Anthony Gould have just 27 catches as a whole, it puts things into perspective.
However, this presents huge opportunities for the top three receivers.
Dulin has been mostly a special teams ace in Indianapolis, but now gets a shot to be possibly the top pass-catcher out of nowhere.
Treadwell can get more playing time as a starter than perhaps he's ever seen throughout his 11 years in the league.
Burks will immediately become the top deep threat for the Colts, and will also get work in the slot after the Downs trade.
This offense was already in deep trouble with Downs and Allen on the field, so things could get even more dicey for the passing game and quarterback Daniel Jones.
Regardless, while it gives Dulin and Treadwell the chance as starters, perhaps none of these players will benefit more from the thin wide receiver room than Burks.

title: Colts GM Vacancy Became More Attractive After Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' general manager vacancy looked like a difficult proposition when Chris Ballard was relieved of his duties in October . The team was struggling, the roster was headed for a significant overhaul, and Indianapolis doesn't own its 2027 first-round draft pick.
However, the Colts' activity at the NFL trade deadline has changed the outlook considerably . Indianapolis parted ways with four established starters, accumulated additional draft capital, and created an opportunity for its next general manager to reshape the roster.
There is still plenty of work to be done, but the resources and flexibility now available could make Indianapolis a more appealing destination for potential candidates than it was just a few weeks ago.
One of the biggest selling points of the Indianapolis job is the collection of resources the next general manager will have at his disposal. Between additional draft selections and projected salary-cap flexibility, the Colts have several avenues to begin rebuilding their roster.
Indianapolis currently owns 10 selections in the 2027 NFL Draft, before compensatory picks have been awarded. OverTheCap projects the Colts to receive two more picks , a fith-rounder and sixth-rounder, though that's yet to be confirmed. Still, the prospect of having a dozen selections should be attractive.
Additionally, Indianapolis holds eight more picks in 2028 following its trades. The Colts acquired six total picks in those four transactions while surrendering one seventh-round selection to Kansas City in the Josh Downs deal .
While Indianapolis does not own a first-round pick in 2027 after including its selection in the trade for Sauce Gardner at last year's deadline, the volume of additional selections gives its next general manager plenty of opportunities to fill the roster with players that fit his or her style.
The Colts also have the flexibility to package selections to move up the board or pursue established players through the trade market. No shortage of options with it comes to utilizing draft capital.
There is also the financial component to consider.
Indianapolis is currently projected to have approximately $48 million in salary-cap space for the 2027 season, according to OverTheCap . That figure could change as the offseason approaches, but it gives the next general manager considerable financial flexibility to pursue free agents, retain key contributors and address the roster's most glaring deficiencies.
The quarterback situation could provide another opportunity to create financial flexibility. Daniel Jones currently carries a projected $46.8 million cap hit for 2027, making his future one of the most consequential financial decisions facing the organization. Jones has played nowhere close to the level the Colts paid him to play at, making a parting of ways the most likely outcome in the offseason.
Releasing Jones with a post-June 1st designation would clear up to $38 million in cap space, leaving $86 million in total for the next regime to use at their discretion.
The combination of additional draft capital and significant projected cap space gives the next general manager multiple ways to approach a rebuild. Rather than being restricted to the draft or free agency, Indianapolis can use both avenues to accelerate its roster reconstruction.
Perhaps just as important as the resources available to Indianapolis' next general manager is the freedom to determine what the roster should look like moving forward.
The Colts have already begun their locker room overhaul, but several significant decisions remain. The most notable involves Jonathan Taylor, who surprisingly remained in Indianapolis despite considerable trade interest leading up to the deadline.
Multiple teams reportedly offered a second-round pick or better for the three-time Pro Bowl running back, but Indianapolis ultimately held onto its franchise player. That decision now leaves Taylor's future in the hands of the next general manager.
There is a legitimate argument for keeping Taylor and building around one of the league's most productive running backs. However, there is also a case for moving him while his trade value remains high, particularly with Indianapolis entering a rebuilding period that could extend beyond the remainder of his prime.
Either way, the next general manager will have the freedom to decide what to do with Taylor. He can evaluate his value to the organization, determine whether his timeline aligns with the team's plans and decide whether another trade attempt makes sense.
The same flexibility exists at quarterback.
Jones remains in Indianapolis after the trade deadline, but his long-term future is far from settled. The Colts can evaluate whether he is the right quarterback to lead the next iteration of the franchise or whether it makes more sense to pursue another option through the draft or free agency.
There is also the possibility of giving Anthony Richardson another opportunity, depending on how the new leadership evaluates his future with the organization.
Beyond those two positions, the next general manager will have considerable freedom to determine which remaining veterans fit the team's long-term plans and which young players deserve further opportunities to establish themselves.
That level of autonomy is an important selling point for any potential candidate.
All that said, Indianapolis is certainly not an easy job. The roster has significant deficiencies, the team is coming off a disappointing season and the next general manager will have their work cut out for them to turn the franchise around.
However, the Colts have positioned themselves to offer something that isn't always available to incoming front-office executives: the resources and freedom to build an organization in their own image.

title: Colts Biggest Winners and Losers From 2026 NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts underwent a significant roster overhaul during the NFL trade deadline, parting ways with four prominent contributors in an effort to accumulate draft capital and reshape the franchise's future.
After trading away defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and left guard Quenton Nelson earlier in the season, Indianapolis dealt wide receivers Keenan Allen and Josh Downs on Tuesday.
The four moves leave considerable holes on both sides of the football, but they also create opportunities for several players who remain in Indianapolis.
Some players stand to benefit from expanded roles and increased responsibilities, while others are left with considerably less support as the Colts attempt to navigate the remainder of a disappointing season.
Here are the biggest winners and losers from Indianapolis' trade deadline activity.
The Colts' decision to trade both Keenan Allen and Josh Downs leaves a wide receiver room devoid of established playmakers, creating an opportunity for Ashton Dulin and Deion Burks to see more involvement in the offense.
Dulin is the more experienced option of the two, having been in Indianapolis since 2019. He's mostly been a special teams asset, but has stepped into a larger offensive role as they years have gone by.
Meanwhile, Burks is the more interesting of the two. He has an opportunity to establish himself as a more consistent contributor and show what he can offer moving forward. The seventh-round pick hasn't seen too many opportunities thus far, logging just nine touches so far, but will have a chance to prove he can be in the mix for the slot receiver job moving forward.
With Indianapolis already looking toward the future, their performances over the remainder of the season could help determine where they fit into the team's plans.
DeForest Buckner's departure created a significant opportunity along the interior defensive line, and few players stand to benefit more than Adetomiwa Adebawore.
Adebawore has already emerged as one of Indianapolis' most promising defensive players, earning a two-year, $35 million contract extension after establishing himself as a legitimate disruptive presence up front.
Now, with Buckner no longer in the picture, an even greater responsibility falls on the young defensive tackle.
Adebawore's first game since signing his new deal demonstrated he can handle that burden. The 25-year-old didn't record a sack, but showcased a multitude of effective pass rush moves and helped influence the pocket numerous times, resulting in teammates finishing the play.
The Colts will need Adebawore to become a centerpiece of their defensive front, particularly as they begin transitioning toward a younger roster. His development was already an encouraging storyline before the deadline, but Buckner's departure gives him an opportunity to take another significant step forward.
Quenton Nelson's departure leaves enormous shoes to fill along the offensive line, but it also opens the door for rookie guard Jalen Farmer to establish himself as a long-term starter.
Farmer has already stepped into Nelson's vacated spot, with a mixed bag of results through two games. Still, moving on from Nelson makes the remainder of the season an important evaluation period for the fourth-round selection.
Replacing a player of Nelson's caliber is an enormous challenge, but the opportunity to gain valuable starting experience should benefit Farmer's development.
With Indianapolis entering a period of transition, the organization needs to identify which young players can become foundational pieces moving forward. Farmer now has an opportunity to make a strong case for himself as part of the team's next iteration along the offensive line.
Grover Stewart's inclusion here is a little different from the other winners, considering his contract expires at the end of the season. His status as a winner hinges significantly on whether or not he signs an extension to be a part of the rebuilding process.
The veteran defensive tackle had been mentioned as a potential trade candidate, and the Colts had offers on the table. However, Indianapolis ultimately elected to keep him, leaving Stewart as one of the most experienced players remaining along the defensive front.
With Buckner gone, Stewart's importance to the defensive line becomes even greater. His ability to provide stability against the run and serve as a veteran presence alongside younger players should be valuable as the Colts navigate the remainder of the season.
Whether Stewart ultimately factors into Indianapolis' longer-term plans remains uncertain, particularly with his contract situation, but he should have an important role to play in the immediate future.
While Daniel Jones remains the Colts' starting quarterback, the circumstances surrounding him have become considerably less favorable.
Indianapolis traded away two of its most productive receivers while also sending away its All-Pro left guard. That's a substantial amount of offensive talent to lose, particularly for a quarterback who has already struggled to find consistency throughout the season.
The Colts haven't exactly surrounded Jones with an abundance of established weapons following those departures, leaving him with fewer reliable options as the offense attempts to finish the season strong. For a quarterback who's best seasons came when he had an adequate supporting cast, the deadline trades greatly hurt his ability to lead an offensive revival down the stretch.
Jones now faces the challenge of producing with a significantly diminished supporting cast while the organization evaluates its direction at quarterback.
Jonathan Taylor might be the biggest loser of the Colts' trade deadline .
For weeks, Taylor was at the center of trade rumors as Indianapolis explored its options ahead of the deadline. Multiple contenders expressed interest in acquiring the three-time Pro Bowl running back, and the Colts reportedly received multiple offers involving second-round draft capital and more.
Despite the interest, Indianapolis ultimately decided against moving him, holding out for a blockbuster return that never materialized.
That decision leaves Taylor in a difficult position. The Colts have made it abundantly clear that they're transitioning toward a rebuild. But Taylor is entering the latter portion of his 20s and remains one of the most productive running backs in football.
There's a legitimate concern that Indianapolis won't be ready to compete for a championship again until Taylor is past his prime. Barring a future trade request or a dramatic turnaround in the team's trajectory, he could spend at least the next two seasons wasting away on a team in transition.
It's difficult to blame Taylor for wanting to remain in Indianapolis, particularly after signing a contract extension in the offseason and repeatedly stating his loyalty to the organization. But the Colts' decision to retain him despite multiple trade offers leaves one of their best players tied to a rebuilding franchise.
Running back's primes are limited, and it's possible Taylor doesn't get anything substantial out of his.
Perhaps nobody was dealt a more difficult hand at the trade deadline than head coach Shane Steichen.
The Colts have traded away four prominent starters, including two foundational offensive players, while also removing a significant talent from their defensive front. The result is a considerably less experienced roster with multiple holes that need to be addressed.
Steichen, already facing an uphill battle to save his job, now faces the challenge of keeping Indianapolis competitive while evaluating younger players and attempting to get the most out of a diminished roster. That's not exactly a formula that will help Steichen stay on as head coach.
With Chris Ballard already dismissed and Indianapolis preparing for a new general manager, Steichen must demonstrate that he's the right person to lead the franchise moving forward.

title: Grading Colts' NFL Trade Deadline: Fire Sale Provides Solid Start to Rebuild
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has officially passed, and the Indianapolis Colts made it clear what direction this franchise is heading.
At 2-7 and riding a five-game losing streak, the Colts have spent the last two weeks turning expiring contracts into draft capital while refusing to sell off everyone on the roster.
So, did Indianapolis get enough value? Let’s grade every move.
This is still the one I have the biggest problem with.
Nelson is one of the best guards of this generation, and getting only a 2027 third-round pick and 2028 fifth-rounder feels light. That being said, he was on an expiring contract, and paying him another massive deal at 30 years old probably did not fit where this rebuild is heading.
Not only did he not quite fit into the rebuild's outlook, but Nelson did manage to net the most draft capital for a guard in recent memory. According to Spotrac, via Alex Katson, Nelson is the only traded guard since 2011 to net a third-round draft selection .
I still would have wanted an earlier pick. The difference between what Indianapolis got for Big Q and what other teams have received for All-Pro talent is pretty staggering.
I don’t mind this one nearly as much.
Buckner is 32, was on an expiring deal, and likely would not be the same player by the time Indianapolis is ready to seriously compete again. Getting a 2027 fourth-round pick while sending him back to a contender makes sense.
Allen was on a one-year deal, and Indianapolis turned a 34-year-old receiver into a 2027 sixth-round pick. San Francisco needed receiver help, and the Colts took advantage.
This changed right before the deadline.
Downs requested a trade after the Nelson and Buckner moves, and Indianapolis sent him plus a 2027 seventh-rounder to Kansas City for 2027 fourth- and fifth-round picks.
Considering Downs' poor performances over the last few weeks, I'm surprised the Colts got as much as they did.
For an expiring-contract player who wanted out, that is solid value.
I applaud this front office for not getting taken advantage of here.
Multiple teams were reportedly willing to offer a second-round pick and more, but Taylor is under contract through 2028 and did not request a trade. If nobody wanted to overpay for one of the league’s marquee running backs, keep him.
I’m glad to see No. 28 stay.
Jones has not played well, and Indianapolis reportedly told him before the deadline that he would not be moved. I still believe Jones can look serviceable when the pieces around him are right, but this team has failed to give him that consistency this season.
Adebawore has emerged as one of Indianapolis’ premier young defenders, and locking him up through 2028 gives this rebuild a legitimate piece to build around. He entered Week 9 leading NFL defensive tackles in both pressure rate and pass-rush win rate.
This front office did a solid job turning expiring contracts into picks without getting desperate on Taylor.
I still would have rather kept Big Q, but considering the situation Dodds inherited, I think Indianapolis made the best of a difficult situation.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Instant Grade: Understanding Colts' Decision to Keep Jonathan Taylor
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts were at the epicenter of the 2026 NFL Trade Deadline after they kicked off an early rebuild by firing longtime general manager Chris Ballard .
The Colts subsequently traded franchise pillars LG Quenton Nelson and DT DeForest Buckner for draft capital, which led to a fire sale watch of sorts manned by interim general manager Ed Dodds.
From players on expiring deals to those with multiple years left on their contract, the Colts' roster featured no untouchables, though running back Jonathan Taylor was treated as the next best thing.
After weeks of rampant rumors surrounding the star running back, the Indianapolis Colts have decided to hold onto their star running back as they enter a new era.
Taylor is still one of the league's best running backs and is undeniably the Colts' best remaining player, but was this the right move? Follow along as I break down the decision in question.
The Indianapolis Colts remained steadfast in their pursuit of a Christian McCaffrey-esque return , one that included three current draft picks (2nd, 3rd, and 4th) as well as a future fifth-round pick, for Jonathan Taylor, but the return simply never came calling.
The New York Giants were reportedly the biggest contenders of the sweepstakes in question, as their offer of a 2027 second-round pick, a fifth-round pick, and an unnamed player was turned down, but the Colts stayed firm in their belief in Taylor.
But it wasn't just the Giants who came calling and/or offered similar compensation. Outside of the Giants, the reported interested teams were the Green Bay Packers, Denver Broncos, Minnesota Vikings, Seattle Seahawks, and Cincinnati Bengals.
Furthermore, the Colts had received multiple offers of a second-round pick and more for Taylor over the last week, according to NFL Insider Jordan Schultz .
"But the [Colts] decided that if they ever trade him, it will be in the offseason, when more buyers could be available and a permanent general manager is in place," Schultz reported.
The Colts set a price on a player they valued highly, and when the demand wasn't met, they decided to table talks until at least the offseason.
Will Indianapolis be better off for it? There's certainly an avenue that suggests they make the correct decision, especially considering how quick turnarounds happen in the NFL, but the Colts are embarking upon a massive rebuild, one that likely won't find its footing in time for Taylor's services to matter.
Nothing will change in terms of personnel at the position, but the Colts' immediate outlook at offense looks bleaker than it ever has since Jonathan Taylor joined the team in 2020.
The Colts still have Taylor to lean on for the rest of the 2026 regular season, but considering they've since traded away their best player and blocker across the offensive line, as well as their second and third-best options at wide receiver, and are continuing to roll with Daniel Jones at quarterback, it's hard to imagine a world where Taylor finds sustainable success.
Indianapolis will continue rolling with a two-man backfield of Jonathan Taylor and rookie Seth McGowan for the rest of the year, so even though risking Taylor's health in a lost season is a big chance to take, at least the rookie won't be baptized by fire down the stretch.
Carlie Irsay-Gordon has shown a rather strong process in her first full season as the Indianapolis Colts' principal owner and CEO.
Irsay-Gordon pulled the plug on the past era mere months after she decided to run it back once more with general manager Chris Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen, and this seemingly abrupt move to rip the band-aid off was no easy decision.
Since they lost to the winless Tennessee Titans in Week 5, the Colts have fired Chris Ballard, extended their most promising up-and-coming player (Adetomiwa Adebawore), and have traded four players on expiring deals.
In one month, Irsay-Gordon and Co. have set up the Colts' rebuild via a sound process.
However, the Colts' decision to keep Jonathan Taylor around for the foreseeable future is a questionable one.
On one hand, the Colts were open to trading Taylor. Their decision to ultimately keep Taylor wasn't a case of delusional belief in a player, but rather a strategic attempt to net top-tier compensation while also leaving the door open for the next general manager if demands weren't met.
The issue with this notion is that the Colts are entering a legitimate rebuild that will likely require multiple years to iron out. Not only that, but the Colts are also risking Taylor's health as they prepare to let their new general manager make his/her first big decision.
Taylor would not only have to stay healthy to justify this decision, but he'd also have to perform like the top-tier running back that he is down the stretch to increase, or even maintain, his current trade value.
Given that the aforementioned current-look Colts offense is devoid of talent everywhere else, coupled with the fact that Indianapolis' season is lost, it's difficult to imagine a reality where Taylor can produce to the level we know he's capable of.
Running backs have a shelf life that typically comes calling around ages 27-28, and given that's the range Taylor is in, on top of him playing in arguably the league's worst offense, a regression feels inevitable.
Taylor's recent extension from earlier this offseason puts him under contract through the 2028 season, and since the Colts have already paid him his signing bonus, Taylor's cap hits for the next two seasons are very reasonable.
Providing the next brass with the option to keep Taylor makes the job more attractive on the surface, as they can either roll with a Top 5 running back in the NFL or move him for draft capital.
However, if the next regime decides that an aging running back is a building block of the future, then we already know how the next era will go. Perhaps this will serve as a day-one test for the next general manager, but it still feels like a missed opportunity to start anew.
Jonathan Taylor is still elite, but he hasn't been playing like it in recent weeks, and that was in an offense that has since been depleted even more.
Overall, Irsay-Gordon and Co. have done a good job kicking off the Colts' rebuild in question. Only time will tell if their belief in Taylor will end up hurting them.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Instant Grades: Colts Get Strong Return From Josh Downs Trade
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have officially moved on from Josh Downs, sending the 25-year-old wide receiver to the Kansas City Chiefs in exchange for a pair of 2027 draft picks.
Indianapolis will receive a fourth-round pick and a fifth-round pick, sending Downs and a seventh-round pick back to Kansas City.
Trade terms: 4 and 5 for Downs and a 7, per source. https://t.co/vC2Yc7mzlE
It's a strong return for a player who had requested a trade, was approaching the end of his rookie contract, and clearly wanted out of Indianapolis. More importantly, the Colts managed to improve upon the compensation that had initially been circulating around the league.
Here's an instant look at the deal and what it means for Indianapolis moving forward.
The Colts initially placed a third-round valuation on Downs, but reports throughout the past few weeks suggested that interested teams were willing to give up a fourth-round pick at a maximum. Reports indicated that the Colts had a fourth-round pick offer on the table from the Chiefs a week ago.
But rather than immediately accepting that proposal, Indianapolis allowed the market to develop and ultimately secured an additional fifth-round selection, sending a seventh-rounder back for Kansas City to take on Downs' remaining contract.
Downs was unlikely to sign an extension with the Colts in the offseason, so turning him into usable assets for the future was a necessary move to make.
Downs was selected in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft and established himself as a productive slot receiver during his first few seasons. He recorded 72 receptions for 803 yards and five touchdowns in 2024, demonstrating the ability to become a reliable underneath option in the Colts' passing attack.
However, his production has declined since then. Downs finished his Indianapolis tenure with 33 receptions for 354 yards and one touchdown through nine games in 2026.
There were also growing concerns about Downs' commitment to a struggling team. Since requesting a trade, Downs appeared increasingly apathetic towards the situation in Indianapolis, making a separation the only logical course of action for both sides.
The Colts ultimately turned a disgruntled receiver in the final year of his rookie contract into two draft selections. Getting an additional Day 3 pick on top of the reported fourth-round market is a win for Dodds and the Indianapolis front office.
The only real downside is what Indianapolis is left with at wide receiver. After moving on from Downs and Keenan Allen on deadline day , the Colts have likely the ugliest receiving corps in the NFL. Alec Pierce remains the most established option, but he's been on injured reserve for the majority of the season. After him, there's no remaining proven talent.
Still, that's a relatively minor concern given the direction of the organization. Indianapolis has bigger priorities than maintaining a competitive receiving room for the remainder of a lost season, and the draft capital acquired in these transactions gives the franchise additional resources to address those needs.

Still, that's a relatively minor concern given the direction of the organization. Indianapolis has bigger priorities than maintaining a competitive receiving room for the remainder of a lost season, and the draft capital acquired in these transactions gives the franchise additional resources to address those needs.
The Colts couldn't have asked for a much better outcome given the circumstances surrounding Downs' departure.
They secured two draft picks for a receiver who was in the final year of his rookie contract, had requested a trade and had struggled to produce consistently during a difficult season. Indianapolis also appears to have benefited from allowing the trade market to develop rather than settling for the initial fourth-round price tag.
The return is strong, the timing makes sense and the organization can now move forward without another lingering distraction. I'm docking a letter grade solely due to the messy state of the current WR room, but again, that's nothing to stress about in the bigger picture.
In the end, the Colts turned a difficult situation into a productive transaction---exactly what they needed to do at the deadline.

title: Indianapolis Colts Fire Sale Tracker: Analysis, Trades, Rumors, and More
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts will be the center of the NFL world for the foreseeable future.
This is the second consecutive season that Indianapolis will be featured in trade talks at the midway point, but unlike last year, it's not because they're the number one seed in the AFC.
Instead of buying at the deadline, the Colts will be selling.
The 2026 NFL Trade Deadline (November 10th, 4 PM EST) is quickly approaching, and the Colts are amidst a complete teardown of their franchise.
The Colts fired longtime general manager Chris Ballard after they fell to 2-4 in a humiliating loss, and have been active in the trade market ever since as they look to recoup any valuable draft capital they can after Ballard traded away their 2027 first-round pick, as well as their 2026 first-rounder and WR Adonai Mitchell.
It was the beginning of a poetic end, as the last Ballard-led Colts game was a loss to the 0-5 Tennessee Titans, a team that many still consider the worst team in the NFL. Even then, this version of the Colts may very well be the league's worst.
On top of only one playoff win in three appearances, the Colts failed to win the lowly AFC South across 9.5 seasons (2017-2026) under Chris Ballard.
Despite ample evidence to suggest otherwise, Indianapolis Colts' Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon decided to bring back both Chris Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen for the 2026 season, referencing their hot start to the previous year as a reason to give them another chance.
The former had been given far too many chances to that point, but to be fair to Irsay-Gordon and her sisters, Co-Owners Kalen Jackson and Casey Foyt, this was the organization's first full offseason under new ownership.
Following the decision to give Ballard and Steichen one last shot in her postseason press conference, Irsay-Gordon said that the "sense of urgency has never been higher" for the GM/HC tandem.
Many didn't believe her, given that she was entering her first full offseason as an NFL Owner/CEO and appeared to be betting on an inevitable collapse, but Irsay-Gordon did what needed to be done, even if it came a bit too late.
In the past 14 days, the Indianapolis Colts have fired longtime general manager Chris Ballard, fallen to 2-6 on the season, and traded away two of their franchise cornerstones.
This article is meant to serve as a one-stop shop for all things Indianapolis Colts-related ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline. I will be updating this story as new information presents itself, so be sure to regularly check back in.
Navigate our trade central (finalized trades, rumors, etc.), future outlook, and more below.
Outside of players still on their rookie contract, as well as some exceptions such as cornerback Sauce Gardner, wide receiver Alec Pierce, left tackle Bernhard Raimann, and a few others, nobody on the Colts roster is safe.
Although the 2026 NFL Trade Deadline is on November 10th at 4 PM EST, the Colts have already gotten a head start on their fire sale.
In order, our trade central will featured finalized trades, a rumor mill, and will conclude with analysis on the team's overall outlook.
A current third-round pick and a future fifth-rounder may seem scoff-worthy at first glance, but when you break down the history of traded compensation for other guards across the league, Nelson's haul starts to make more sense.
Indianapolis' return of a 3rd and a 5th for Quenton Nelson is the most pure draft capital for a guard since at least 2011, per Spotrac. only 4 have netted a 4th: 2013: G. Carimi, 4th 2014: L. Mankins, 4th + player 2021: B. Bredeson + 5th + 7th, 4th 2025: J. Thuney, 4th
I think this is both the best example of why the return for Quenton Nelson isn’t as irresponsible as some are suggesting, and also why the Chris Ballard era needed to end: non-premium positions.
It stings to see any team trade their homegrown future Hall of Famer, but this is the bed the Colts made, and now they must sleep in it.
The Colts' 2026 fourth-round rookie guard Jalen Farmer is Nelson's immediate replacement.
Buckner's departure creates a similar challenge on the defensive line. More responsibility will fall on the remaining interior defenders, including Stewart and Adetomiwa Adebawore.
Not only is the opportunity there, but Adebawore has earned the increased role in question.
After seven weeks, Adebawore is undeniably the Colts' best pass rusher. He is currently tied for second with the most sacks among interior defensive linemen league-wide and leads the team in most major pass-rush statistics.
We've known that Adebawore has some nasty pass-rushing chops, but the biggest development has been his improvement in run defense.
Adebawore has blossomed into a legitimate starting defensive tackle, and it comes at no better time as the Colts have parted ways with their longtime pillar across the defensive line.
However, the Colts' newfound star is on an expiring deal. Adebawore is playing in the final year of his rookie contract, so a big payday is set to come his way.
Update (11/3) : The Indianapolis Colts have signed Adetomiwa Adebawore to a two-year, $35 million contract extension that includes a $13 million signing bonus and $22.5 in new money through 2027.
The Colts had seemingly found their third starting wide receiver for the 2026 regular season after they signed veteran free agent Keenan Allen to a one-year deal late in training camp.
Allen has been productive for the Colts, as his 40 receptions lead the team, and his 351 receiving yards are second only to Josh Downs, another Indianapolis wideout who is likely to be traded ahead of the deadline. He was only meant to serve in a secondary role alongside Alec Pierce and Josh Downs, but the former's aggravated injury forced the 34-year-old veteran into a serious role.
Allen sits at 27th all-time in receiving yards (12,402) and 8th all-time in receptions (1,095) as he moves back out West to the contending 49ers.
The Indianapolis Colts managed to get fantastic value for a wide receiver who is on an expiring deal, has been checked out as of late, and plays a hyper-specific role. Indianapolis had reportedly been looking for a third-round pick in return, but netting two early Day 3 (rounds 4-7) is still a massive win.
After weeks of nonstop rumors, the Colts have decided to keep their most productive player from the Chris Ballard era as they enter their rebuild. An offer of a second-round pick plus additional compensation was not enough to get done, though it probably should have been.
Taylor will be 28 years old and will have two years left on his contract when the Colts enter a new era, and given that their offensive outlook looks even bleaker than it has, it's hard to imagine a world where he can improve the Colts' floor.
The Colts are willing to revisit trade talks for Taylor once the next general manager is in the building, though I doubt they're able to warrant better, if not similar, compensation than they could have at the deadline. I figured the failed Ballard era would have resulted in the Colts going in a new direction as far as roster construction goes, but time will tell if they've made the correct decision.
Update (11/5) : NFL Insider Jordan Schultz : "The belief around the league is that, barring an offer that blows them away, Indianapolis plans to wait until after Sunday’s game vs the Cowboys before revisiting the offers on the table and making the trades that make sense on Monday and Tuesday ahead of the deadline.

Schefter added that the Colts have already received an offer of a 2027 second-round pick along with additional compensation for Taylor's services.
