title: LIVE: Titans NFL Trade Deadline Tracker With Trades, Rumors, and Updated News
full_text:
We're now just a little over four hours out from the NFL trade deadline. At this point, we've exhausted our predictive brains and are waiting on the Tennessee Titans to either make a move or stand pat when the 3:00 PM CT cutoff strikes.
As of this morning, our latest update came in the form of a confirmation from Jordan Schultz: Tennessee is not looking to move RB Tony Pollard. He's become almost too crucial to Cam Ward and the offense to be sent packing at the midway point this season.
However, it's worth noting that Albert Breer said it would take "at least a fourth-rounder, and maybe a third" to get Pollard out of Nashville. Breer also admitted that Tennessee "won't give him away," but a different source setting a price there is notable.
If the Colts ultimately refuse to trade Jonathan Taylor, Pollard's value could skyrocket at the buzzer. Past Pollard, the Titans' outlook is mostly up in the air. WR Calvin Ridley still looks like a definite possibility, while S Amani Hooker also appears to be in the currently safe camp with Pollard.
That trio set aside, DE Jermaine Johnson is a name fans should keep an eye on. There has been minimal noise surrounding Johnson, but he's in the final year of his contract and could be argued as an asset worth moving for the Titans to stack more draft capital. LB Cody Barton should be tabbed for similar reasons.
It's straw-grasping from there. We'll keep you looped in as news comes in today, Titans fans. Check back here for the latest.
(12:21 PM) Could Mitch Trubisky be a surprise candidate for the Vikings?
Adam Schefter reported that the Vikings have "begun making calls" earlier today in search of a QB. With Kyler Murray injured and Carson Wentz leading the team to an underwhelming loss in primetime last night, could Mitch Trubisky be a sneaky option?
The Titans have already made it clear that Cam Ward is the guy from here on out; if something were to happen that Ward loses his starting gig next season, it isn't like Trubisky would then step into the starting spotlight for the long haul.
Trubisky is a veteran QB who has been biding time on Tennessee's bench all season. In the midst of today's ongoing dry spell of news, it's worth keeping a possibility like this in the back of our minds. If Minnesota goes shopping, a multi-year signal caller with no current shot at playing is prime trade material.
The Titans could realistically make this happen, even if Trubisky's name has yet to come up.
(12:38 PM) Keenan Allen Trade Potentially Sets Price for Calvin Ridley
Per Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport, the Colts are sending WR Keenan Allen to the San Francisco 49ers for a sixth-round pick.
For those keeping an eye on Ridley's market, the Titans' ask of a sixth-rounder for Ridley appears to be right on the money, if not a little expensive now given Allen's superior production. With the 49ers off the board for Ridley, the Chiefs and Steelers are two teams to watch closely.
The deadline is about two hours out now. A move like this could light the fuse for more momentum at the WR position, and Ridley now even more centered in that pool of players.
(1:14 PM) Titans Trade S Amani Hooker to Bills for second and fifth-round pick
Per Tom Pelissero, the Titans have traded S Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills. Tennessee will reportedly return a second-round pick, and send the Bills a fifth.
Trade! The Titans are sending standout safety Amani Hooker to the Bills, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . pic.twitter.com/yHu5GwkjcF
We talked about undeniable offers potentially prying players that the Titans didn't want to trade, and Buffalo delivered just that. For a 28-year old defender, a second-round snag would've been hard for Tennessee to turn down.
Although, the move does mark the loss of the NFL's leader in INTs (five) and another one of the Titans' most notable defensive leaders. Robert Saleh's unit takes another serious hit, but the franchise are loading up on draft value for a fast-tracked rebuild.
The Hooker trade ended up being the final move Tennessee would make prior to the deadline. Jordan Schultz reported that both the Broncos and Giants were interested in Pollard, but the Titans held firm to their belief that he's pivotal to Cam Ward's development.
That hold makes sense. Holding Calvin Ridley, on the other hand, is a loss for Tennessee. After being heavily mentioned all week, Ridley didn't get so much as a mention until four minutes prior to the deadline. That was when Albert Breer said he (as well as Pollard) wouldn't be traded.
Looking back, the Titans dealt arguably their two best defenders. The offensive side of the ball went untouched. Tennessee will be three early picks richer heading into the second half of the 2026 season.
Not a promising omen for the final nine games this year, but the Titans will have a better chance than most low-ranking teams to improve quickly in the next few seasons.

title: 1 Final Prediction: Forecasting the Landing Spot, and Haul, for Titans' Leading Trade Candidate
full_text:
It's become increasingly obvious that if the Tennessee Titans are going to try to move anyone today, it's pass-catcher Calvin Ridley. Sure, we could see a surprise offer come in for one of Tennessee's numerous pieces of defensive depth, or a team could get desperate and throw something crazy out there for RB Tony Pollard.
But as of right now, Ridley is the only name that keeps coming up as one that the Titans would be open and willing to part with. Now tha t the trade deadline is just a few hours away, news regarding this potential move could pop at any time.
Past the likelihoods and the expectations, though, is a deal that actually has to get done. We circled three suitors as primary candidates to trade for Ridley earlier this week; the Kansas City Chiefs, the Pittsburgh Steelers, and the San Francisco 49ers.
Now that another round of football has been played, I'm making the argument that one of those teams has pulled away. In today's last-second prediction, I have the Kansas City Chiefs sending Tennessee a sixth-round pick to secure Ridley prior to the deadline.
The stars are aligning for this move, and it makes sense for either side.
Rising receiver Xavier Worthy left Kasnas City's Week 9 victory over the New York Jets with a hamstring injury, exasperating the team's need at WR to an even further degree. The Chiefs had just returned leading pass-catcher Rashee Rice after he missed multiple weeks earlier this year.
WR Tyquan Thornton is on IR due to a severe ankle injury he sustained earlier this season; backup options Jeff Caldwell and Jimmy Holiday are also off the board. That leaves Kansas City with little choice but to add to that dwindling room.
Ridley may not have a place in Brian Daboll's offense any longer, but a move west could offer the 31-year old new life. Where the Titans are drafting and signing younger talent for their WR core as a part of an overarching rebuild, the Chiefs are grasping at a (mostly) bygone era of success to try and win another championship.
Their franchise makeup is opposite to Tennessee's. Where the Titans are tearing old pillars down, the Chiefs are gluing and taping them together to try and squeeze another title run or two out of the rubble.
Thus far, it's worked. Kansas City is 6-2. But with the Chiefs openly looking to get stronger at WR, per Zachary Pereles, it's clear they're currently short of the intended mark. The sixth-round asking price for Ridley emerged earlier this week as a sign that Tennessee is ready to move on from him.
Kansas City can certainly afford that tag, and if they strike out on someone like Brian Thomas Jr., taking a flyer on Ridley could be their easiest remaining choice. I think it's more likely than not that we see Ridley moved today, and I'm projecting Kansas City as his eventual destination.

title: Addition by Subtraction: How Titans’ LB Room is 1 Trade Away From an Upgrade
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans enjoyed a bye in Week 9, but will get back to work in Week 10 against the Jacksonville Jaguars. However, before Sunday's home contest, Tennessee will need to make decisions on the futures of multiple veteran players.
With the Titans sitting at 1-7 and the trade deadline set for Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET, general manager Mike Borgonzi has gotten plenty of calls on the team's veteran pieces who could provide value to contending squads. The common names mentioned in trade discussions have been running back Tony Pollard, safety Amani Hooker, and wide receiver Calvin Ridley.
One player who hasn't been brought up in trade rumors is linebacker Cody Barton, which is surprising. Barton should be one of Tennessee's top trade candidates ahead of the deadline, as moving on from the veteran linebacker makes a ton of sense.
Barton has been a serviceable starter for the Titans this season, tallying 34 tackles and 16 defensive stops with a 62.4 Pro Football Focus grade . As a result, the former Denver Bronco could net Tennessee a solid return on the market, and trading him makes sense given the state of the linebacker room.
Cedric Gray set the Titans franchise record in combined tackles in 2025 with 164. However, Gray has been demoted to a limited rotational role this year, as rookie Anthony Hill Jr. is the starter next to Barton. Though he has endured some of the usual rookie growing pains, Hill has shown promise this year as a potential long-term starter on the Titans' defense. The Texas product has already posted 82 tackles and 24 defensive stops in eight games , but has struggled in coverage.
Regardless, Hill is a defensive piece Tennessee can build around, and it would be wise for the Titans to roll into the future with him and Gray as the starters. Barton's experience is a nice plus, but Gray is more talented, better in pass coverage, and should be the starter.
Barton doesn't offer much upside for the future, and it's strange that head coach Robert Saleh and defensive coordinator Gus Bradley are playing the 29-year-old over the high-potential Gray. As a result, Tennessee should be shopping Barton and looking to send him to a linebacker-needy team to clear the way for Gray to reclaim his starting spot.
We'll see whether Barton is still on the Titans roster after 4 p.m. ET Tuesday. Barton isn't a negative on Saleh's defense, but Gray should be seeing more reps next to Hill.

title: 10 Commanders Quotes Show Washington’s Close Losses No Longer Count as Progress
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have spent a lot of time talking about how close they are. The 20–13 loss to the Rams left them at 2-5-1, three games behind the New York Giants. After a 27–27 tie in their first meeting , Thursday’s rematch can cut that gap to two games or stretch it to four. Jayden Daniels called it a must win after Sunday's loss. Dan Quinn has avoided that label, but by Wednesday he had little patience left for explanations about new coaches and changing personnel. Lucas Patrick is out , Nick Allegretti is back at center, and the Giants' blitz awaits them again. The week's answers keep coming back to what Washington has to execute: finishing drives, protecting Daniels, defending the Giants' playmakers and getting the late-game details right. From Sunday's postgame interviews through Wednesday's final practice, these 10 quotes show what the Commanders are taking into the Giants game.
Question: How can Washington keep Malik Nabers from beating the secondary deep without letting him pile up yards underneath? “I think that's just—it starts with knocking the run game out, putting them in situations where we know they have to pass the ball. And then, depending on whatever coverage we're taking, understanding what's going to stress our coverage out based off of their concepts, making sure we're all in the right spots. And then from there, just making sure we're tackling him. He's very good with the ball in his hand. He's very elusive, kind of like a running back a little bit. So just being able to get him down when he does have the ball, and of course stay over top, keeping a roof on our coverage.”
Question: Does the possibility of moving two games behind the Giants with a win or four behind with a loss add pressure this week? “You feel the weight of the NFL all the time, right? There's always pressure from, first, a personal standpoint. We have to individually play well and then from a team standpoint. And then you throw media on top and all that, too. Like, there's always pressure from every direction, as you can see. People in contract years, all these little factors that play into it. So no matter what, we're going to have the most pressure on us.”
Question: What has Washington changed to turn red-zone trips into touchdowns instead of field goals? “It's one of the keys that we talked about today, the importance of that, of scoring into the red zone and not having to settle for field goals. So different locations on the red zone, like where shot plays take place compared to crossing ones when you get closer to the goal line, knowing you don't have the distance to go. So having plans to, this is against man-to-man, this is against zone. The decision-making process happens quickly. So how do you recognize what you're seeing and then go attack it? That's what we're working hard on. We've added some extra repetitions for red zone over the last, well now going into the second week of that. That's one of the adjustments that we're making, put the time and the attention on it.”
Question: How do Daniels' suggestions to offensive coordinator David Blough show up in the plays Washington runs on game day? “I think just stuff I don't like throughout the week, he'll take out. Stuff I really do like, he'll call and things like that. So I think that's really where it's shown. And like I say, he's still growing as a coordinator, first-time coordinator, still going through his growing pains and stuff like that. So I just try to do the best I can, just go out there, execute. Doesn't matter what the play call is. It doesn't matter anything. If we got all 11 people going in the same direction, we have a chance.”
Question: With Allegretti returning to center , what challenges come with another switch in the middle of the offensive line? “Yeah, I mean, little nuances and stuff like that, but I still have trust in Nick. We have a really good relationship, and so from that standpoint, I'm comfortable playing next to him.”
Question: After Sunday's Rams loss, how urgent is it to turn the season around against New York? “Yeah. I think next week is a must win.”
Question: How much do a new coordinator, new system and personnel changes explain Washington's late-game failures? “I'd say we're all frustrated. We wanna get to the bottom of that and get the things correct that we want. So I'd say our time on task, there might be new people. Some of the situations, they're not that different and familiar. So we've got to be able to nail these, honestly. That's where we are at the halfway point. And so no excuses on that part. This is part of the gig and how we have to get it done, and we have to get these done.”
Question: What's the difference between playing with urgency and playing desperately? “Desperate is like you're just hoping. You're just hoping. I mean, urgent, like you have a plan ... We need to accomplish it now versus desperate is like, ‘All right, guys, let's just hope. Let's just see what we can do.’ We're not in that stage right now. So definitely urgency.”
Question: Why has Allegretti spoken openly about working with mental-health coaches while dealing with injuries and moving in and out of the lineup? “Just because of how much it helped me. It's one of those things that, as men, we're lulled into this, ‘Don't talk about it. Handle your things yourself.’ And I tried for a long time and I got to a point where it was too much for me. And I'll say probably one of the reasons that I handled the day-to-day here well when I'm not playing is just all the people that were here for me, helped me get the help that I needed. Not just in the locker room, but some coaches, staff members really went out of their way to make sure I was right. “It's a process, obviously. Still working weekly with that, but it's something that in life I never thought I would need to work on. You lift weights, you recover, you work on the football, you watch film, you do all this stuff, but you don't really ever work on the mental health side of things. So really proud of myself and appreciative of my teammates that encouraged me to take that step. Appreciate you asking.”
Question: At what point does saying the Commanders are close to a complete game stop being enough? “I mean, now, right? I mean, what's the point of being close? We eight games in, so either you figure it out or you going to continuously find yourself in the same position having these same conversations, trying to get the same results. So figure it out now. ... It's not time to be trying to figure out, ‘Oh, we're almost there. Almost there. Almost there.’ Either you're there or you're not.”

title: Commanders-Giants Final Injury Report: Lucas Patrick Out, Treylon Burks Expected Back Despite Missed Practice
full_text:
Lucas Patrick is out Thursday night against the New York Giants. The Commanders’ final injury report also ruled out tight end Colson Yankoff, leaving Washington to start Nick Allegretti at center in place of Patrick. Burks’ place on the active list will be confirmed with Thursday’s inactives. Yankoff did not practice during the short week because of a knee injury. Daniels (left elbow) and Gulbin (knee) practiced fully throughout the week. title: The Commanders Found a Deep-Ball Role for Treylon Burks Worth Keeping
full_text:
The NFL isn't like basketball, where prospects land on depth charts before a wide role gets eventually thinned out, nor is it similar to other team sports like baseball or hockey with their substantially longer seasons of potential opportunities. Development in a game with minimal room to overtake starters and even less leeway to change positional archetypes places an exceptional amount of weight on preexisting infrastructure, with a potentially poor response to a specific environment often getting misconstrued as analysts attempt to understand the players before them.
As we now know, Treylon Burks is one of those players who needed more of a push in a specific direction than he got. The Tennessee Titans hoped he'd become the franchise's playmaker for years to come when they drafted him with the first-round pick acquired in the A.J. Brown trade with the Philadelphia Eagles, but the Washington Commanders have been happy to get consistent production out of him since signing him to their practice squad a little over a year ago.
It's becoming increasingly clear that his ascendance as a go-ball artist has far more to do with his partnership with Jayden Daniels than it does with the X-spot opened up by the down-for-the-count Terry McLaurin. Despite his long path here and his still-incomplete game, he's as worthy of a full-time starting gig as he ever has been, a necessary bright spot during a team-building period that's badly searching for wins.
To be clear, he didn't shift from a disappointing former first-round pick into a relied-upon wideout overnight. It took him most of last year to finally impress Washington and its frustrated fan base. He didn't have much time to build chemistry with Daniels, as the quarterback appeared in only two of the Commanders' 10 final matchups. Burks did, however, enjoy a moment in the sun when he made one of the team's top plays of the season: a fading one-handed touchdown grab against one of last season's top defenses, the Denver Broncos.
#Broncos CB Riley Moss... got Moss'd. Treylon Burks, man. This is incredible. pic.twitter.com/mmK0TeTW4x https://t.co/KZdkroMomU
Though little from that late-season stretch offered any long-term guarantees, he still seemed worth monitoring whenever the Commanders next meant business.
A few months later, when it was time for the squad to whittle its training camp participants down to an inner circle of rotational playmakers, he had 130 yards over eight games to lean on, not much, but enough to convince management that his 13 yards per reception offered some upside as a deep-ball threat, something they lacked outside of the aging and battered McLaurin. Burks himself hadn't exactly been Mr. Perfect Attendance, having yet to make a dozen appearances in a season, with a mere five outings logged during his final year in Tennessee, but his talent made a flier seem worth it.
Washington's play-callers have leaned all the way in on Burks and the long ball, spiking his yards per target to a career-high 10.6 on 22 targets over a half-dozen-game sample size. 19.4 yards per reception also rings in as a high-water mark thanks to the work he's doing after his tough catches, and his average nightly yardage count of 38.8 is within two ticks of the 40.4 mark he'd once peaked at as the Titans' hyped rookie.
Updated WR separation & Catchpoint/YAC Grades pic.twitter.com/mX4vSuk3xm
He's drawing some of the deepest targets at his position, proving a unique enough threat to keep on earning trust from Washington's staff. Following his first target attempt in Week 8 against the Eagles, a bobbled pass he dropped from point-blank range, the Commanders went back to him four more times for 81 yards on three receptions in a successful gamble.
McLaurin's absence after a torn patellar tendon suffered last month has opened a starting spot to complement slot options like Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams. Daniels has his groove back thanks to a more versatile receiving corps, and his stabilizing presence as a dual-threat creative is proving that Burks may have even more to unlock beyond his role-player status, let alone as a must-deploy ahead of pure reserve options like Luke McCaffrey and Dyami Brown.
Look no further than the Commanders' most recent outing, a Burks-less 20-13 loss to the Los Angeles Rams , for evidence of how much it hurts to lack that extra help. After being left alone with a thin corps of Diggs, Williams, Chig Okonkwo, and surprise hero Van Jefferson, Burks' combination of physical force and finesse will be appreciated when he returns from his foot injury for Thursday's Giants rematch in New York.
With D.C. serving as a "second draft" for the former washout, he's looking almost as deserving of attention as a true rookie like Williams, thanks to his unique skill set. Washington should keep that downfield role for him even when the receiving corps gets healthier. It only took some time to unlock, and the Commanders may have plenty more of that coming as they navigate another messy season.

title: Commanders Power Rankings Fall After Rams Loss, but Dan Quinn Faces a Bigger Question
full_text:
Each week during the regular season, we'll look at what the national media is saying about the Washington Commanders via various publications' NFL Power Polls. With it being Week 10, the chances of winning the division or making the playoffs are starting to look thin. The Washington Commanders followed their best win of the season with another frustrating loss , falling 20-13 to the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday and dropping to 2-5-1. That didn't do Washington many favors with the national media. Six of the nine publications we track each week moved the Commanders down in their latest power rankings, including one writer who had a much different opinion of this team just seven days ago. * Side note: Many have asked whether these polls are helpful, which is a fair question. One way to look at them is as a way to broaden your perspective on what others believe. Not to mention, sometimes it's fun to see the national media guys bump around in the dark, chasing their tails, clueless.

Sports Illustrated - No. 22
Sports Illustrated - No. 28
Note : The table above links each poll to the corresponding publication name. Remember last week when Sports Illustrated's Conor Orr was calling Washington his favorite to win the NFC East? Well, apparently that didn't last long. Orr dropped the Commanders six spots after Sunday's loss, taking them from No. 22 to No. 28. That's quite a turnaround in seven days, although watching Washington stumble through another late-game situation probably didn't help. Oddly enough, ESPN actually moved Washington up a spot despite the loss. WalterFootball still has the Commanders at No. 18, while CBS Sports and Sports Illustrated have them sitting at No. 27 and No. 28, respectively. Hard to find much agreement there, other than the fact that Dan Quinn has some serious work to do. There's something else worth pointing out this week. Six of the nine publications brought up Dan Quinn's job security, which tells you just how much the conversation has changed around Washington. ESPN's John Keim says Quinn's seat could become "white-hot" with another loss Thursday, while NFL.com's Nick Shook believes it's time to start watching for potential coaching changes. Mike Florio at Pro Football Talk went even further, suggesting the mini-bye following the Giants game could be the time to make a move; of course, Florio has repeatedly said Quinn's seat was hot since the preseason. That's a lot of attention on a head coach whose team was being picked by at least one national writer to win the division just a week ago. Quinn certainly hasn't helped himself with some of the late-game decisions we've seen , but Thursday's matchup against New York suddenly carries more weight than just another game in the NFC East standings. The Commanders need a win, and their head coach could probably use one even more. Last week’s Power Ranking Index : No. 24 HIGHEST Ranking: No. 18 LOWEST Ranking: No. 28 Last week’s result : Lost to the Los Angeles Rams 20-13 This week : @New York Giants ESPN had this to say (24th): With their current record, the Commanders are quickly running out of time to stick around in the NFC East. Because they tied the Giants last month, they could earn the tiebreaker with a win. Of course, they would still have to win a few other games down the stretch to make the playoffs. But they'd be alive mathematically. The bigger issue is that if they fall to 2-6-1, coach Dan Quinn's seat will become white-hot. The third-year coach needs to be much better after a 5-12 record in 2025. -- John Keim
CBS Sports had this to say (27th) The heat is getting hotter on the seat underneath Dan Quinn as they move to the final nine weeks. They are pretty much done. — Pete Prisco NFL.com had this to say (26th) Sunday provided yet another discouraging result for a Washington team that still doesn’t take care of the details or handle end-game scenarios well. It’s only the midpoint of the season, but it’s time to put the Commanders on watch for potential coaching changes. They simply don’t have enough to climb out of this hole, not with the way they’re playing. — Nick Shook
Fox Sports had this to say (26th): Jayden Daniels is playing better, which is good, and he tried to pull off a miracle comeback against the Rams. But he just doesn’t have enough horses around him to ride to his team’s rescue anymore. The Commanders have been decimated by injuries, and with shortages at RB and WR, it’s like Daniels is their only weapon. And that’s just not enough against teams like the Rams. Maybe they’ll have better luck at the Giants on Thursday night, but good luck keeping up with the Bengals after that. It’s really already another lost season in Washington. The only question is how long Dan Quinn can survive. — Ralph Vacchiano Sports Illustrated had this to say (28th): I think if there was a team that didn’t need to be the focal point of an end-of-game situational football occurrence gone awry, it would be the Washington Commanders. Alas…   — Conor Orr
Yahoo Sports had this to say (24th): Jayden Daniels set the stakes for Thursday night's game against the Giants, when asked after the team's loss to the Rams whether time is running out to get back in the NFC East race. "Yeah. I think next week is a must-win," Daniels told reporters after the game. He's right. With a win, the Commanders would be two games behind the Giants for first place and hold the tiebreaker, since the teams tied in their first meeting. That's not easy, but Washington wouldn't be dead. If the Commanders lose, they'd be four games back and not have the tiebreaker, which would probably be impossible to overcome. It might not matter because the Commanders aren't very good — they're 20th in DVOA with matching ranks of 20th on offense and defense — but at least with a win they'd have something to keep playing for.  — Frank Schwab Pro Football Talk had this to say (26th) The mini-bye could be the time to bid farewell to the head coach. — Mike Florio The Athletic had this to say (26th) A bad division was there for the taking for Dan Quinn and the Commanders. But they haven’t just found ways to lose (or tie) games. They’ve done it in a comical fashion that has raised questions about Quinn and Jayden Daniels’ game management. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Walter Football had this to say (18th) How in the world does Dan Quinn still have a job? I don't understand how this team continuously screws up in late-game situations. One of these debacles is bad enough, but the Redskins keep making the same mistakes and embarrassing themselves.
Put all nine together, and the Commanders land at an average ranking of No. 25.0, down from last week's 23.8. Washington doesn't have much time to worry about what the national media thinks, either. Thursday night's rematch against the New York Giants is coming fast, and another loss would leave the Commanders at 2-6-1 with eight games remaining. At that point, the conversation around this team could look considerably different. We'll revisit these each week and see where the national pulse moves next. Washington ranks 11th in rushing yards per game and 25th in attempts, while its 31.13% third-down conversion rate is the worst in the NFL . The Commanders converted three of 12 against the Rams and ran only 10 plays in the third quarter. Quinn sees more carries coming from longer drives. title: Commanders’ Must-Win Giants Rematch Hinges on Replacing Five Players From the Tie
full_text:
The last time the Washington Commanders and New York Giants played, the game ended in a 27-27 tie after both teams missed chances to win in overtime. That day, Stefon Diggs was inactive, and Jer'Zhan (Johnny) Newton was on injured reserve. Terry McLaurin , Dyami Brown, Daron Payne, Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt, and Javon Kinlaw played; all five are now on IR. A month later, Washington has managed only one win since, and will enter the game at 2-5-1 after losing 20-13 to the Rams in Week 9. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn acknowledged the importance of Thursday's game during his presser on Monday: "But what I will say is, like, man, we need this win this week. There’s no doubt." Washington heads to MetLife Stadium this week three games behind the 5-2-1 Giants in the NFC East, where another loss would push Quinn’s team further out of the race.
McLaurin caught four passes for 62 yards in the first meeting, while Brown played 23 offensive snaps. Diggs gives Daniels another proven receiver against New York, but getting him involved has been an issue of its own. He finished with three catches for 51 yards on 38 offensive snaps against the Rams. “So he’s definitely, like, in the front of our thinking. And so we need him, you know,” Quinn said about Diggs Monday. Washington needs that thinking to turn into completions before it’s chasing the game in the final minutes. Van Jefferson has a much bigger part in this offense now, too. He played just three offensive snaps against the Giants, compared with 36 against Los Angeles, where he caught five passes for 58 yards and a touchdown. Antonio Williams’ workload has grown from 42 snaps in the tie to 52 against the Rams. Jefferson should stay involved even if Treylon Burks returns from the foot injury that kept him out Sunday. He gave Blough another weapon to work with. The backfield has changed as well. Croskey-Merritt ran for 82 yards and a touchdown on 11 carries in the first meeting. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler handled the running-back snaps against the Rams. I’d get both involved early Thursday and make New York account for them as runners and receivers. Blough has to find production there alongside everything he’s asking of the wideouts.
🚨 TOUCHDOWN COMMANDERS 🚨 BILL CROSKEY-MERRITT IS GONE 💨 Washington takes an early 7-0 lead vs. the Giants! pic.twitter.com/RDAz8I7XNg
Daronte Jones has two substantial workloads to replace up front. Payne played 63 of Washington’s 89 defensive snaps in the tie, while Kinlaw played 56. Payne also recorded a sack and a forced fumble. With both players now on IR , Washington will ask a different group to handle the interior work and create some disruption of their own. Newton’s return to the lineup helps, but his first game back also shows how much work falls on the rest of the rotation. He played 20 defensive snaps against the Rams , while Shy Tuttle played 43, Tim Settle 33, and Ricky Barber 15. I’d keep sharing that work, with Newton’s workload based on what he’s ready to handle. Getting him back gives Jones another option; it doesn’t fill both openings on its own. Blough has to get production from a different supporting cast, and Jones has to make this rotation hold up for four quarters. That’s the job Thursday. Quinn’s staff needs useful contributions from the players available now, with little room left for another game that ends in explanations. title: Commanders Daily: Washington Was Short on Receivers. Where Was Stefon Diggs?
full_text:
Heading into the Rams game on Sunday, the Washington Commanders were short on receivers: Terry McLaurin is out for the season, Treylon Burks is out, and Dyami Brown moved to injured reserve. Sounds like a day for Stefon Diggs to shine, right? The problem is Diggs' first catch, a four-yard burner, came with 7:28 left in the third quarter; he wouldn't gain another yard until a five-yarder with 4:41 left in the game. With 52 seconds remaining, they found him again for a 42-yard catch that moved Washington from its own 9 to the Rams' 49 and put the team in position to tie the game. When asked Monday why Diggs only had the one catch entering the final five minutes, Quinn responded by saying, "Yeah. I love his fire, man. Ben, I really do. And the competitive part. So he hit a couple targets earlier, and some that maybe he’s also first in the read to get there. Or for whatever reason, you know, you have to get off that. Or, you know, the read wasn’t there; the coverage took you somewhere else. So he’s definitely, like, in the front of our thinking. And so we need him, you know. And so that’s why he’s in the front of our thinking in those critical spots. So, you know, certainly one towards the end, you know, that gives us a chance to go after it. But, no, he’s always in the front of our thoughts. I love his fire. I love what he brings. And, like most excellent players, like as many opps as you can." Quinn is saying Diggs was the first read on some plays and that coverage pushed Daniels elsewhere on others. That is the politically correct response, but it still doesn't explain why Diggs had only four yards with five minutes left.
"You wish them nothing but the worst" 🤣 Stefon Diggs weighed in on how aware he is of the Commanders place in the NFC East. pic.twitter.com/WqWdICiBQT
After McLaurin’s injury, Quinn said he didn’t expect Diggs’ workload to increase much and pointed to rookie Antonio Williams as a player in line for more opportunities. The snap counts from the Rams game check out: Diggs played 38 of Washington's 62 offensive snaps against Los Angeles, while Williams played 52 and Van Jefferson had 36. Diggs had played 39 of 60 snaps against Philadelphia a week earlier, when Burks and Brown were both available. Even with those two out against Los Angeles, his snap share stayed about the same. Asked whether the two- and three-tight-end packages were why Diggs played less in the first half, Quinn said it wasn’t part of a deliberate design. Diggs missed the first game against New York that ended in a 27-27 tie, meaning Thursday will be his first game against the Giants in the burgundy and gold. The question is: Can Washington connect with Diggs earlier on the opportunities intended for him? His 42-yarder showed what one connection could change, but it arrived with less than a minute left against Los Angeles, a team without its top two cornerbacks .
Stefon Diggs giving the #Commanders life with this 40 yard play pic.twitter.com/U8WGIBxUJt

title: Hughes’ View: The Commanders’ Center Gamble Left Jayden Daniels Exposed
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have hit that point in the season where, at 2-5-1, it's over unless they start winning, and the Giants and Cowboys have a massive fallout. Which could happen, but shouldn't be depended on under normal circumstances. For Washington, they have to ask themselves, how did they get here? Their latest issue on the offensive line stems from the center position: this past weekend, when their starter Lucas Patrick went down with a concussion, they turned to rookie Matt Gulbin. It's ironic because Adam Peters and Dan Quinn spent the offseason trying to convince everyone that Nick Allegretti was that guy and would be the center for 2026. Allegretti has played two snaps since his last start, which came at right guard against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 3. In other words, he's still the same journeyman offensive lineman who came here years ago looking for a chance to start, but better suited as a backup. They tried to sell the fanbase a pumpkin, hoping Cinderella logic would kick in and he'd turn into something more than a dried-up gourd that rots on a warm fall night.
To understand this mistake in motion, you first have to remember that the team's center in 2025, Tyler Biadasz, was abruptly released before free agency, not long before the team struck out on free agent Tyler Linderbaum , who signed with the Raiders. That led the team to Allegretti as the answer, even though he played only 78 NFL snaps at center before 2025 and then started the final two games that season. No reason has ever been given for Biadasz being cut, and Peters dodged rehashing any of it in all of his offseason pressers, but Peters' plan beyond Linderbaum was clearly flawed. After roster cuts, Peters said , "And that's where we went into this offseason feeling that Nick could be our starter, and still do feel that way." Drafting Gulbin in the sixth round may prove to be a great move in the future, but what about protecting your franchise quarterback now? The problem looked at least temporarily fixed when Lucas Patrick stepped into the role against Seattle . Washington had signed Patrick just 11 days before that start. In that game, right guard Sam Cosmi couldn't go, so it made sense to slide Allegretti over. The next week in London, Patrick stayed at center, and Gulbin slid over to right guard. That signaled Patrick had already taken over for the offseason starter, though Quinn initially called the change temporary before naming Patrick the starter the following Friday.
When asked about the situation Sunday after the game , Quinn said the staff has been working Allegretti more at guard now: "In that moment, I would have felt comfortable with Nick as well, but I thought, let’s give the guy who’s got the most reps." Quinn also confirmed Allegretti was healthy. It makes sense that the coach would turn to the player who has practiced the most in the role; the problem is he said this in the preseason: "Nick is one of our smartest players, so that's a position that you rely on." Relied on so much that when the team looks for a replacement weeks later in crunch time with the season on the line, they turn to the sixth-round prospect with very little experience. Gulbin gave up a 12-yard sack to Myles Garrett on third-and-5 at the Rams’ 38, leaving Washington facing fourth-and-17, but who could be mad at a rookie who should have been given more help on that play? The Commanders' protection plan failed when it mattered most Sunday; that's not to say there wasn't effort; it is to say the coaches didn't do their jobs.

Thursday night in New York will tell us whether anybody learned from this. Patrick is in concussion protocol, and Quinn has three days to decide who gets the next snap and what kind of help he’ll have. The Giants are leading the division. They won’t wait while Washington figures it out on the fly. If the rush gets home again because the staff leaves its center on an island, Daniels will be the one paying for decisions he didn’t make. Nine games left sounds hopeful until your quarterback spends the first of them running from the same problem you promised was solved.
